units.text: Melanotan II is approved for no therapeutic indication. US: FDA's compounding safety page (current as of 22 April 2026) lists it among nominations withdrawn from Category 2, citing impurity and immunogenicity risks and published reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism. UK: MHRA (FOI 24/274, 17 April 2024) classes injectable products as medicines, says unauthorised medicines may not be sold, supplied or advertised, and advises users to stop immediately. Australia: TGA (17 August 2026) — prescription-only medicine, not approved as a tanning agent, no product on the ARTG.

assertions.text: Melanotan II is not approved for any therapeutic indication.
assertions.quote: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic α‐MSH analogue that is a nonselective MCR agonist and is not approved for use in any therapeutic indication.
assertions.note: Supported by the literature review on MC1R activation.

assertions.text: The US FDA compounding safety page (as of 22 April 2026) lists Melanotan II among nominations withdrawn from Category 2, citing impurity and immunogenicity risks and published reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome, and priapism.
assertions.quote: Compounded drugs containing Melanotan II may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation or peptide-related impurities. Published case reports discuss serious adverse events including melanoma, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism.
assertions.note: Supported by the FDA Category 2 bulk drug substances web page.

assertions.text: The UK MHRA (FOI 24/274, 17 April 2024) classifies injectable Melanotan II products as medicines.
assertions.quote: Products containing Melanotan II are classified as medicines if they are injectable or pens.
assertions.note: Supported by the MHRA FOI response.

assertions.text: The UK MHRA advises users to stop using Melanotan II immediately and states that the sale, supply, and advertising of unauthorised medicines is not permitted.
assertions.quote: These products may cause serious side effects, so our advice to those who have used Melanotan II injections or nasal sprays is to stop using them immediately and if you have suffered side effects, speak to your doctor and report them to the MHRA through our Yellow Card Scheme.
assertions.note: Supported by the MHRA FOI response.

assertions.text: In Australia, the TGA (17 August 2026) states Melanotan II is a prescription-only medicine, not approved as a tanning agent, with no product on the ARTG.
assertions.quote: Melanotan II is a prescription-only medicine in Australia and is not approved for use as a tanning agent. There are currently no products containing Melanotan II included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) or approved for supply in Australia.
assertions.note: Supported by the TGA safety advisory.

units.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats a personal or family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II. A case report describes crops of new atypical naevi and growth of existing naevi in a man with prior melanoma who self-injected an α-MSH analogue, with lightening after he stopped; MC1R activation does not prevent melanoma, and regular skin examination remains critical in high-risk people.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats a personal or family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II.
assertions.quote: causation is unproven, but the mechanism (proliferation of melanocytes, including neoplastic clones) makes it a real concern, and a personal or family history of melanoma is an absolute contraindication.
assertions.note: The guide states that a personal or family history of melanoma is an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II.

assertions.text: A case report describes crops of new atypical naevi and growth of existing naevi in a man with prior melanoma who self-injected an α-MSH analogue, with lightening after he stopped.
assertions.quote: A 40-year-old white man with a history of melanoma and multiple dysplastic nevi self-administered synthetic alpha-MSH. He developed crops of new pigmented nevi, many of which had atypical clinical and histopathologic features. The preexisting nevi became darker and acquired growth features. After alpha-MSH use was discontinued, the nevi progressively lightened and lost their growth features.
assertions.note: The case report describes these clinical findings following self-administration and discontinuation of synthetic alpha-MSH.

assertions.text: MC1R activation does not prevent melanoma, and regular skin examination remains critical in high-risk people.
assertions.quote: MC1R activation through induction of UV‐protective skin pigmentation increased DNA repair, and control of aberrant cell growth may reduce the risk of melanoma but importantly does not prevent melanoma particularly in individuals with risk factors and regular skin examination remains critical in high‐risk individuals.
assertions.note: The review emphasizes that MC1R activation does not prevent melanoma and regular skin examination remains critical in high-risk individuals.

units.text: Skin monitoring matters with melanocortin agonists: during Melanotan II use, sequential videodermoscopy documented naevus changes that made naevus and melanoma hard to tell apart, and even the approved MC1R agonist's US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.

assertions.text: During Melanotan II use, sequential videodermoscopy documented naevus changes that made distinguishing between a naevus and melanoma difficult.
assertions.quote: The changes of patient's nevi were documented by sequential videodermoscopy before and during treatment. The observed dermoscopic changes made it difficult to differentiate a nevus from a melanoma.
assertions.note: Mang et al. (2012) documented that sequential videodermoscopy during Melanotan II treatment showed changes making it difficult to differentiate a nevus from melanoma.

assertions.text: The US label for the approved MC1R agonist recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.
assertions.quote: A full body skin examination (twice yearly) is recommended to monitor pre-existing and new skin pigmentary lesions.
assertions.note: The Scenesse US prescribing information recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly to monitor pigmentary lesions.

units.text: PTD-DBM is a cell-penetrating peptide that competes CXXC5 off Dishevelled, activating Wnt/β-catenin; in mice it accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced follicle neogenesis, and CXXC5 is raised in human balding scalp. This single 2017 study from the developer's group is its whole evidence: no human trial is published (PubMed) or registered (ClinicalTrials.gov) as of 24 September 2026. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

assertions.quote: Disrupting the CXXC5-Dishevelled interaction with a competitor peptide activated the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that disrupting CXXC5-Dishevelled interaction with the competitor peptide activated the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.

assertions.text: In mice, competitor peptide treatment accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis.
assertions.quote: Disrupting the CXXC5-Dishevelled interaction with a competitor peptide activated the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis.
assertions.note: The study abstract states that the competitor peptide accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced hair follicle neogenesis.

assertions.text: CXXC5 is upregulated in human balding scalp.
assertions.quote: CXXC5 was upregulated in miniaturized hair follicles and arrector pili muscles in human balding scalps.
assertions.note: The study abstract confirms CXXC5 upregulation in human balding scalps.

assertions.text: The single 2017 study from the developer's group is PTD-DBM's whole evidence, with no human trials published or registered as of 24 September 2026.
assertions.quote: Clinical caveat. Mechanistically the most interesting investigational hair-loss compound on this list, but human efficacy data is thin — most use is via compounding pharmacies. Effective only combined with a Wnt-pathway modulator (typically valproic acid). Trial stage: preclinical only; no human RCTs.

units.text: Thymulin is a thymic peptide that is biologically active only when zinc-bound. No indexed human study of zinc thymulin for hair was found (the Peptide Pocket Guide's cited case series could not be located); its proposed hair mechanism is undefined, and whether any effect comes from the peptide or the zinc is unresolved. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

assertions.text: In the UK, afamelanotide has a marketing authorisation under exceptional circumstances for preventing phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, and is to be prescribed only by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres.
assertions.quote:
Afamelanotide has a marketing authorisation in the UK under 'exceptional 
circumstances' for the 'prevention of phototoxicity in adult patients with 
erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)'.
assertions.note: NICE HST27 confirms that afamelanotide holds a UK marketing authorisation under exceptional circumstances for this indication and stipulates prescribing only by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres.

assertions.text: NICE guidance HST27 (published 26 July 2023) did not recommend afamelanotide for use in the NHS.
assertions.quote:
Taking into account all of the evidence and factors affecting the decision, afamelanotide is 
not recommended for use in the NHS.
assertions.note: NICE HST27 concluded that afamelanotide is not recommended for NHS use.

units.text: In the UK, a medicine made up for one patient without a marketing authorisation is an unlicensed 'special'; MHRA guidance says an unlicensed product should not be used where a UK-licensed product could meet the patient's need, and special need excludes cost, convenience and operational reasons.

assertions.text: In the UK, an unlicensed medicinal product specially prepared or imported for an individual patient without a marketing authorisation is referred to as a 'special'.
assertions.quote: This Guidance Note provides advice on the manufacture, importation, distribution and supply of unlicensed medicinal products for human use (commonly described as “specials”) which have been specially manufactured or imported to the order of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber for the treatment of individual patients.
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 confirms that unlicensed medicinal products manufactured or imported for individual patients are commonly described as specials.

assertions.text: MHRA guidance states that an unlicensed product should not be used where a UK-licensed product could meet the patient's need.
assertions.quote: An unlicensed product should not be used where a product available and licensed within the UK could be used to meet the patient's special need.
assertions.note: MHRA guidance explicitly specifies that an unlicensed product should not be used if a product licensed and available within the UK can meet the patient's need.

assertions.text: Under MHRA guidance, justification of 'special need' excludes reasons of cost, convenience, and operational needs.
assertions.quote: The requirement for a “special need” relates to the special clinical needs of the individual patient. It does not include reasons of cost, convenience or operational needs (see Section 10 of this guide).
assertions.note: MHRA guidance clarifies that special need relates strictly to clinical need and excludes cost, convenience, or operational reasons.

units.text: Growth hormone acts mainly in the dermis: its receptor is expressed more by dermal fibroblasts than keratinocytes, and GH increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, acts on keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor; in culture IGF-1, not GH, drives keratinocyte proliferation.

assertions.text: Growth hormone activity in the skin is primarily evident in the dermis, where it supports collagen synthesis.
assertions.quote: GH activity, sometimes mediated via IGF-I, is primarily evident in the dermis, particularly affecting collagen synthesis.
assertions.note: Edmondson et al. note that GH activity is primarily evident in the dermis and affects collagen synthesis.

assertions.text: The growth hormone receptor is expressed at higher levels in dermal fibroblasts than in keratinocytes.
assertions.quote: Northern analysis, using the cloned GH-R as probe, revealed relatively higher levels of GH-R transcripts in cultured human dermal fibroblasts compared to cultured keratinocytes or keratome biopsies.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. found relatively higher levels of GH-R transcripts in fibroblasts compared to keratinocytes.

assertions.text: Growth hormone increases fibroblast cell numbers.
assertions.quote: In contrast, GH (10 ng/ml) after 5 d markedly increased fibroblast cell numbers (70%, p less than 0.009) over 0.2% serum control.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. observed that GH significantly increased fibroblast numbers.

assertions.text: IGF-1 is produced locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, whereas keratinocytes abundantly express the IGF-1 receptor.
assertions.quote: mRNA transcripts for the major mediator of GH actions, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), were detected by PCR in fibroblasts, melanocytes, and keratome biopsies, but not in keratinocytes. In contrast, IGF-1 receptor mRNA were abundant in cultured keratinocytes and skin biopsies, as determined by Northern analysis.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. detected IGF-1 mRNA in fibroblasts and melanocytes (not keratinocytes), while IGF-1 receptor mRNA was abundant in keratinocytes.

assertions.text: In culture, IGF-1, but not growth hormone, promotes keratinocyte proliferation.
assertions.quote: IGF-1 but not GH (5-50 ng/ml) promoted clonal proliferation of cultured keratinocytes.
assertions.note: Tavakkol et al. reported that IGF-1, but not GH, promoted clonal proliferation of cultured keratinocytes.

units.text: Human hair follicles operate a functional peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic (GHRH–GH–IGF-1) axis ex vivo.

assertions.text: Human hair follicles operate a functional peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic (GHRH–GH–IGF-1) axis ex vivo.
assertions.quote: The human hair follicle runs functional peripheral equivalents of the central axes: it synthesizes cortisol and operates a local HPA-like loop,[11] and ex vivo it sustains a hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) that paces its own growth.[12]
assertions.note: The source explicitly confirms that human hair follicles operate an ex vivo functional hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent involving GHRH, GH, and IGF-1.

units.text: GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age (the somatopause); IGF-1 must be read against age- and sex-adjusted ranges, so a value low for a young adult is often normal for age.

assertions.text: GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age, a process known as the somatopause.
assertions.quote: The somatopause is the progressive fall in growth-hormone pulse amplitude and IGF-1, beginning in the third decade and among the steepest of all.[2]
assertions.note: The cited book excerpt directly states that the somatopause is the progressive fall in growth-hormone pulse amplitude and IGF-1.

assertions.text: IGF-1 must be referenced against age- and sex-adjusted ranges, meaning a level that is low for a young adult is often normal for an older individual.
assertions.quote: Reference by age and sex: IGF-1 and DHEA-S decline normally with age — "low-for-young" is often normal-for-age.
assertions.note: The testing checklist explicitly states to reference IGF-1 by age and sex because low-for-young is often normal-for-age.

units.text: Human skin reflects the axis at its extremes: adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis and reduced sweating on biopsy, not fully reversed by treatment of childhood-onset deficiency; in acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema thicken and puff the skin of the face, hands and feet.

assertions.text: Adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis and reduced sweating, changes that are not fully reversed by GH treatment in those with childhood-onset deficiency.
assertions.quote: Importantly, these changes are not fully reversed despite long-term and adequate GH treatment in patients with childhood onset GHD.
assertions.note: Lange et al. demonstrate significantly decreased epidermal thickness and sweat secretion rate in GHD patients, noting these changes are not fully reversed with long-term treatment.

assertions.text: In acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and oedema cause puffiness of the skin of the face, hands, and feet.
assertions.quote: Skin puffiness due to dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and edema are most prominent in the face, hands and feet.
assertions.note: Ben-Shlomo notes that skin puffiness from glycosaminoglycan accumulation and oedema is most prominent in the face, hands, and feet.

units.text: In people with burns over 40% of body surface, recombinant GH shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing in pooled small randomized trials (13 RCTs, 701 people), with more hyperglycaemia; the evidence carries risk of bias.

assertions.text: In pooled randomized trials involving 13 RCTs and 701 people with burns over 40% of body surface area, recombinant growth hormone shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing time.
assertions.quote: There is some evidence that using rhGH in people with large burns (more than 40% of the total body surface area) could result in more rapid healing of the burn wound and donor sites in adults and children, and in reduced length of hospital stay, without increased mortality or scarring, but with an increased risk of hyperglycaemia.
assertions.note: The Cochrane review included 13 RCTs with 701 participants (mean TBSA >40%) and found accelerated burn wound and donor-site healing.

assertions.text: Recombinant growth hormone treatment was associated with increased hyperglycaemia.
assertions.quote: Pooling the studies of adults and children yielded a significantly higher incidence of hyperglycaemia in the rhGH‐treated participants (RR 2.65; 95% CI 1.68 to 4.16).
assertions.note: Pooled analysis showed a significantly higher incidence of hyperglycaemia in patients treated with recombinant human growth hormone.

assertions.text: The evidence on recombinant growth hormone for burns carries a risk of bias.
assertions.quote: This evidence is based on studies with small sample sizes and risk of bias and requires confirmation in higher quality, adequately powered trials.
assertions.note: The review authors concluded the evidence was based on trials with risk of bias and small sample sizes.

units.text: A much-cited 1990 NEJM study gave GH to 12 healthy men over 60 with nine untreated men as comparison and no placebo; skin thickness rose 7.1% (P = 0.07, not significant). A 1996 RCT in 28 older men found 15% more collagen deposited in implanted wound tubes on GH — a laboratory surrogate.

assertions.text: A 1990 NEJM study administered growth hormone to 12 healthy men over 60 with nine untreated men as comparison and no placebo, finding that skin thickness increased by 7.1% (P = 0.07, not statistically significant).
assertions.quote: During the treatment period, 12 men (group 1) received approximately 0.03 mg of biosynthetic human growth hormone per kilogram of body weight subcutaneously three times a week, and 9 men (group 2) received no treatment.
assertions.note: Supported by the 1990 study abstract reporting 12 treated vs 9 untreated men and a 7.1% increase in skin thickness (P = 0.07).

assertions.text: A 1996 RCT in 28 older men found 15% more collagen deposited in implanted wound tubes in those receiving growth hormone compared with placebo.
assertions.quote: Hydroxyproline content was 15% greater in the wounds of the growth hormone group (n = 13) compared with the placebo group (n = 15), (4.52 +/- 0.94 versus 3.92 +/- 0.78 microg/cm; p = 0.04).
assertions.note: Supported by the 1996 RCT abstract finding 15% greater hydroxyproline content in implanted porous tubes in the growth hormone group compared with placebo.

units.text: In healthy older adults, randomized trials of GH show small body-composition changes (about 2 kg less fat, 2 kg more lean mass) with more oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome and gynaecomastia and a trend to diabetes, while strength and endurance change little; GH is not recommended as anti-ageing therapy. A&RE grades this advice A; on the course rule the trials give B, with the same conclusion.

assertions.text: In healthy older adults, randomized trials of growth hormone (GH) demonstrate body-composition changes of approximately 2 kg reduction in fat mass and 2 kg increase in lean mass.
assertions.quote: In participants treated with GH compared with those not treated with GH, overall fat mass decreased (change in fat mass, -2.1 kg [95% CI, -2.8 to -1.35] and overall lean body mass increased (change in lean body mass, 2.1 kg [CI, 1.3 to 2.9]) (P < 0.001), and their weight did not change significantly (change in weight, 0.1 kg [CI, -0.7 to 0.8]; P = 0.87).
assertions.note: Liu et al. (2007) reported an overall fat mass decrease of 2.1 kg and an overall lean body mass increase of 2.1 kg.

assertions.text: GH therapy in healthy older adults is associated with higher rates of oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome, gynaecomastia, and a trend toward diabetes mellitus or impaired fasting glucose.
assertions.quote: Persons treated with GH were significantly more likely to experience soft tissue edema, arthralgias, carpal tunnel syndrome, and gynecomastia and were somewhat more likely to experience the onset of diabetes mellitus and impaired fasting glucose.
assertions.note: Liu et al. (2007) confirmed increased incidence of soft tissue edema, arthralgias, carpal tunnel syndrome, gynecomastia, and onset of diabetes mellitus / impaired fasting glucose.

assertions.text: GH administration alone produces little to no significant improvement in muscle strength and endurance in healthy older adults.
assertions.quote: Sex steroid + GH increased muscle strength marginally and VO( 2)max in men, but women had no significant change in strength or cardiovascular endurance.
assertions.note: Blackman et al. (2002) found no significant improvement in strength or cardiovascular endurance with GH alone.

assertions.text: Growth hormone is not recommended as an anti-ageing therapy in healthy older adults.
assertions.quote: On the basis of this evidence, GH cannot be recommended as an antiaging therapy.
assertions.note: Liu et al. (2007) explicitly concluded that GH cannot be recommended as an anti-aging therapy.

assertions.text: A&RE assigns a Grade A strength of evidence to the recommendation against using growth hormone for healthy aging.
assertions.quote: Growth hormone in healthy older adults is not recommended — modest body-composition changes are outweighed by edema, arthralgia, insulin resistance, and carpal tunnel, and it is illegal to prescribe for anti-aging in the US GRADE A.[6]
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) grades the recommendation against GH in healthy older adults as Grade A.

units.text: In the US (21 U.S.C. 333(e), current text read September 2026), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating a disease or recognized condition authorised by FDA, on a physician's order, is a federal offence.

assertions.text: In the US under 21 U.S.C. 333(e), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating a disease or recognized condition authorized by the FDA/HHS, pursuant to a physician's order, is a federal offense.
assertions.quote: Except as provided in paragraph (2), whoever knowingly distributes, or possesses with intent to distribute, human growth hormone for any use in humans other than the treatment of a disease or other recognized medical condition, where such use has been authorized by the Secretary of Health and Human Services under section 355 of this title and pursuant to the order of a physician, is guilty of an offense
assertions.note: 21 U.S.C. § 333(e)(1) defines knowingly distributing human growth hormone for unauthorized uses without a physician's order as a punishable offense.

units.text: Tesamorelin, a GHRH analogue, reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks in two developer-run phase 3 RCTs (806 patients pooled), with subcutaneous fat unchanged; in the US it has been FDA-approved since 2010 for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy, and its label excludes weight loss. Both guides grade it A — for that indication only.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks with subcutaneous fat unchanged in a pooled analysis of two phase 3 RCTs comprising 806 patients.
assertions.quote: A total of 806 ART-treated HIV patients with excess abdominal fat were randomized in a 2:1 fashion to receive tesamorelin 2 mg (n = 543) or placebo (n = 263) sc daily. At wk 26, VAT decreased significantly in tesamorelin-treated patients (-24 +/- 41 vs. 2 +/- 35 cm(2), tesamorelin vs. placebo, P < 0.001; treatment effect, -15.4%). No significant changes were observed in abdominal sc adipose tissue (-2 +/- 32 vs. 2 +/- 29 cm(2), P = 0.08; treatment effect, -0.6%).
assertions.note: The pooled analysis of 806 patients demonstrated a 15.4% treatment effect reduction in visceral adipose tissue at 26 weeks with no significant change in subcutaneous adipose tissue.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin has been FDA-approved in the US since 2010 for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy, and its label explicitly excludes weight loss management.
assertions.quote: EGRIFTA WR is indicated for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adult patients with lipodystrophy. Limitations of Use: Long-term cardiovascular safety of EGRIFTA WR has not been established. Consider risk/benefit of continuation of treatment in patients who have not had a reduction in visceral adipose tissue. EGRIFTA WR is not indicated for weight loss management as it has a weight neutral effect.
assertions.note: The FDA prescribing information confirms initial approval in 2010 for this indication and states it is not indicated for weight loss management.

assertions.text: Both clinical guides assign tesamorelin a Grade A rating strictly for the HIV-associated visceral adiposity indication.
assertions.quote: Tesamorelin is the instructive exception — a GHRH analog that completed the regulatory path for a defined indication (HIV-associated visceral adiposity) GRADE A, showing what real peptide evidence looks like.[2]
assertions.note: Both guides grade tesamorelin as Grade A specifically for the HIV-associated lipodystrophy/visceral adiposity indication.

units.text: Tesamorelin's label reports IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% (above +3 SDS in 36%) of treated patients at 26 weeks, states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown, reports diabetes-range HbA1c in 5% vs 1% on placebo, lists fluid retention, and contraindicates use in active malignancy.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label reports IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% and above +3 SDS in 36% of treated patients at 26 weeks.
assertions.quote: Among patients who received EGRIFTA for 26 weeks, 47% had IGF-1 levels greater than 2 standard deviation scores (SDS), and 36% had SDS >3, with this effect seen as early as 13 weeks of treatment.
assertions.note: The prescribing information directly reports these exact percentages at 26 weeks.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown.
assertions.quote: The effects of prolonged elevations in IGF-1 levels are unknown.
assertions.note: The prescribing information explicitly states that the effects of prolonged elevations in IGF-1 levels are unknown.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label reports diabetes-range HbA1c in 5% of treated patients vs 1% on placebo.
assertions.quote: During clinical trials, the percentages of patients with elevated HbA 1c  (≥ 6.5%) from baseline to Week 26 were 5% and 1% in the EGRIFTA and placebo groups, respectively.
assertions.note: The label notes that an HbA1c level >= 6.5% occurred in 5% of tesamorelin-treated patients versus 1% on placebo.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin's label lists fluid retention as a warning/precaution.
assertions.quote: Fluid retention: May occur with EGRIFTA WR and may include edema, arthralgia, and carpal tunnel syndrome. ( 5.3 )
assertions.note: Fluid retention is listed under Warnings and Precautions.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin is contraindicated in patients with active malignancy.
assertions.quote: Patients with active malignancy. Any preexisting malignancy should be inactive and its treatment complete prior to instituting therapy [see Warnings and Precautions ( 5.1 )] .
assertions.note: The label explicitly lists active malignancy as a contraindication.

units.text: A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3; the closest human skin data for a GHRH analogue are a 1997 single-blind study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) in 19 older adults, with caliper skin thickness rising after a placebo lead-in and no parallel control.

assertions.text: A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, or IGF-1 LR3.
assertions.note: The provided sources do not describe a September 2026 PubMed literature search evaluating skin outcomes for these compounds.

recheck.note: None of the provided sources mention a September 2026 PubMed search evaluating skin outcomes across tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, or IGF-1 LR3.

assertions.text: In a 1997 single-blind study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) in 19 older adults, caliper skin thickness rose after a 4-week placebo lead-in without a parallel control group.
assertions.quote: Although blood pressure and body weight were unaffected, GHRH analog treatment resulted in a significant increase in skin thickness (P < 0.05) in both genders and increased lean body mass in men only (P < 0.05), with no other changes in body composition or bone mineral density in either gender.
assertions.note: The 1997 study evaluated 10 women and 9 men who received 4 weeks of placebo followed by 16 weeks of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29), observing significant increases in caliper skin thickness.

units.text: CJC-1295 with DAC raised GH and IGF-1 for days in phase 1 trials in healthy adults, with no clinical endpoint; CJC-1295 without DAC ('Mod GRF 1-29') and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies. The Hormonaly guides rate CJC-1295/ipamorelin C ('anecdotal'); on the course rule the evidence for any clinical or skin benefit is D.

assertions.text: CJC-1295 with DAC raised GH and IGF-1 for days in phase 1 trials in healthy adults, with no clinical endpoint.
assertions.quote: After a single injection of CJC-1295, there were dose-dependent increases in mean plasma GH concentrations by 2- to 10-fold for 6 d or more and in mean plasma IGF-I concentrations by 1.5- to 3-fold for 9-11 d.
assertions.note: A phase 1 study in healthy adults showed dose-dependent increases in GH for 6 or more days and in IGF-1 for 9 to 11 days without clinical outcome endpoints.

assertions.text: CJC-1295 without DAC ('Mod GRF 1-29') and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies.
assertions.quote: At the opposite end, CJC-1295 without DAC, PEG-MGF, and IGF-1 LR3 (tier D) have no peer-reviewed human studies and are supported only by preclinical extrapolation and grey-literature user narratives.
assertions.note: The review notes that CJC-1295 without DAC and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies.

assertions.text: The Hormonaly guides rate CJC-1295/ipamorelin C ('anecdotal').
assertions.quote: BPC-157 and TB-500 (largely rodent data),[4] the GH secretagogues CJC-1295 and ipamorelin, and the bioregulators epitalon and thymalin[5] pair plausible mechanisms with mostly anecdotal human use rather than controlled outcome trials GRADE C.
assertions.note: The guide assigns GRADE C to CJC-1295 and ipamorelin due to reliance on anecdotal human use rather than controlled outcome trials.

units.text: Ipamorelin's only efficacy RCT (postoperative ileus, phase 2) showed no benefit over placebo; ibutamoren (MK-677) raised GH, IGF-1 and fat-free mass in a 2-year RCT in older adults without improving strength or function, raised fasting glucose and lowered insulin sensitivity, and a hip-fracture phase IIb trial was stopped early for a heart-failure signal.

assertions.text: A phase 2 randomized controlled trial evaluating ipamorelin for postoperative ileus showed no significant benefit over placebo.
assertions.quote: There were no significant differences between ipamorelin and placebo in the key and secondary efficacy analyses.
assertions.note: The phase 2 trial found no significant difference between ipamorelin and placebo on key efficacy endpoints.

assertions.text: In a 2-year RCT in older adults, ibutamoren (MK-677) increased GH, IGF-1, and fat-free mass without improving strength or functional outcomes.
assertions.quote: Strength, function and quality of life did not improve after administration of MK-677 in this study of a small, healthy cohort.
assertions.note: MK-677 increased GH, IGF-I, and fat-free mass, but did not translate into gains in strength or function.

assertions.text: MK-677 increased fasting blood glucose and reduced insulin sensitivity in older adults.
assertions.quote: Fasting blood glucose increased an average of 0.3 mmol/L (5 mg/dL) with MK-677 (P=0.015) and insulin sensitivity declined.
assertions.note: Fasting blood glucose increased and insulin sensitivity declined in MK-677-treated subjects.

assertions.text: A phase IIb clinical trial of MK-677 in hip-fracture patients was terminated early due to a safety signal for congestive heart failure.
assertions.quote: Trial was terminated early due to a safety signal of congestive heart failure in a limited number of patients.
assertions.note: The hip-fracture trial was stopped early because of congestive heart failure cases in treated patients.

units.text: In the US, sermorelin was approved as Geref (1990, diagnostic; 1997, idiopathic GH deficiency in children), discontinued in 2008, and its approvals withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request; FDA determined in 2013 that this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. As of 24 September 2026 no sermorelin product is marketed (Drugs@FDA), and sermorelin appears in no 503A category (FDA list of 14 May 2026).

assertions.text: In the US, sermorelin was approved as Geref (in 1990 for diagnostic evaluation of GH secretion and in 1997 for idiopathic GH deficiency in children).
assertions.quote: GEREF (Sermorelin Acetate) injection, 0.5 mg base/vial and 1.0 mg base/vial, is the subject of NDA 20-443, held by EMD Serono, and initially approved on September 26, 1997; and GEREF (Sermorelin Acetate) injection, 0.05 mg base/amp, is the subject of NDA 19-863, held by EMD Serono, and initially approved on December 28, 1990.
assertions.note: Supported by the Federal Register determination notice detailing the approval history and indications for both GEREF NDAs.

assertions.text: Sermorelin was discontinued in 2008, and its approvals were withdrawn in 2009 at the manufacturer's request.
assertions.quote: In a letter dated December 2, 2008, EMD Serono notified FDA that GEREF (Sermorelin Acetate) injection, 0.5 mg base/vial and 1.0 mg base/ vial, was being discontinued and requested withdrawal of NDA 20-443; and FDA moved that drug product to the ``Discontinued Drug Product List'' section of the Orange Book.
assertions.note: Supported by the Federal Register notice detailing EMD Serono's 2008 discontinuation letters and withdrawal requests, effective in 2009.

assertions.text: The FDA determined in 2013 that sermorelin was not withdrawn from sale for safety or effectiveness reasons.
assertions.quote: We have reviewed the available evidence and determined that both GEREF products were not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
assertions.note: Supported by the FDA's Federal Register determination.

assertions.text: As of 24 September 2026, no sermorelin product is marketed according to Drugs@FDA.
assertions.quote:
| GEREF
| SERMORELIN ACETATE
| EQ 0.5MG BASE/VIAL **Federal Register determination that product was not discontinued or withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons**
| INJECTABLE;INJECTION
| Discontinued
assertions.note: Supported by the Drugs@FDA listing showing discontinued marketing status for Geref products.

assertions.text: Sermorelin appears in no 503A category on the FDA list of 14 May 2026.
assertions.quote: — Sermorelin — in none of the three categories.
assertions.note: Supported by the 503A roster analysis confirming sermorelin is in none of the three 503A categories.

units.text: US compounding status (FDA 503A category list of 14 May 2026; Category 2 page current 22 April 2026; 21 CFR 216.23 as of September 2026): no GH-axis peptide is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren is in 503A and 503B Category 2; GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 are in 503A Category 3 and 503B Category 2; CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are listed among withdrawn Category 2 nominations, with ipamorelin still in 503B Category 2; FDA's advisory committee voted against ibutamoren (1–13) and ipamorelin (0–12, 1 abstention) in October 2024; a 2020 warning letter named CJC 1295, ipamorelin, IGF1-LR3, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and MK 677 as ineligible for 503A exemptions.

assertions.text: No GH-axis peptide is on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23).
assertions.quote: ( a ) The following bulk drug substances can be used in compounding under section 503A(b)(1)(A)(i)(III) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. ( 1 ) Brilliant Blue G, also known as Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250. ( 2 ) Cantharidin (for topical use only). ( 3 ) Diphenylcyclopropenone (for topical use only). ( 4 ) N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (for topical use only).
assertions.note: 21 CFR 216.23 lists only six substances for use in compounding under section 503A, none of which are GH-axis peptides.

assertions.text: Ibutamoren is in 503A and 503B Category 2.
assertions.quote:
| Ibutamoren mesylate | 503A; 503B | 503A: September 29, 2023
503B: December 29, 2022 | Ibutamoren mesylate poses significant safety risks due to the potential for congestive heart failure in certain patients.
assertions.note: The FDA Category 2 list confirms ibutamoren mesylate is in both 503A and 503B Category 2.

assertions.text: GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 are in 503A Category 3 and 503B Category 2.
assertions.quote: | Growth hormone releasing peptide-2 (GHRP-2) (for injectable and nasal routes of administration) | 503B | September 29, 2023 | Compounded drugs containing GHRP-2 for injectable and nasal administration may pose risk for immunogenicity due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities.
assertions.note: GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 are listed under 503A Category 3 and under 503B Category 2.

assertions.text: CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are listed among withdrawn Category 2 nominations, with ipamorelin still in 503B Category 2.
assertions.quote: | Ipamorelin acetate , which also appears in the table above because it is in category 2 under the 503B interim policy | Compounded drugs containing Ipamorelin acetate may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation or peptide-related impurities.
assertions.note: Both are listed in the withdrawn Category 2 nominations table, and ipamorelin acetate remains in 503B Category 2.

assertions.text: FDA's advisory committee voted against ibutamoren (1–13) and ipamorelin (0–12, 1 abstention) in October 2024.
assertions.quote:
2. VOTE: FDA is proposing that Ibutamoren mesylate NOT be included on the 503A Bulks List. Should Ibutamoren mesylate be placed on the list? 
 
Vote Result:  Yes: 1   No: 13  Abstain: 0
assertions.note: The PCAC October 2024 meeting minutes record the 1-13 vote against ibutamoren and the 0-12-1 votes against ipamorelin substances.

assertions.text: A 2020 warning letter named CJC 1295, ipamorelin, IGF1-LR3, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and MK 677 as ineligible for 503A exemptions.
assertions.quote: For example, the investigators noted that your firm compounded drug products using Follistatin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Endurobal, AOD 9604, BPC 157, Bremelanotide (PT-141), Cerebrolysin, DSIP, Epitalon, GHK-Cu, IGF1-LR3, Ipamorelin, LL-37, Melanotan II, PEG-MGF, Selank, Semax, CJC 1295, SARMS, LGD-4033, and MK 677.
assertions.note: The April 2020 warning letter specifically lists these substances as not eligible for 503A exemptions.

units.text: Skin and soft-tissue signs of GH excess include puffiness and thickening of the face, hands and feet from glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema, oily skin with large pores, hyperhidrosis, skin tags and acanthosis nigricans, with slow acral and jaw enlargement; the Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 measurement for typical acral and facial features and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster (sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, debilitating arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis, hypertension).

assertions.text: Skin and soft-tissue signs of GH excess include puffiness and thickening of the face, hands and feet from glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema, oily skin with large pores, hyperhidrosis, skin tags and acanthosis nigricans.
assertions.quote: Skin puffiness due to dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and edema are most prominent in the face, hands and feet. Oily skin with large pores, hypertrichosis, and excessive sweating are common features. Pigmented skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, and psoriasis are also encountered.
assertions.note: Supported by the review of cutaneous manifestations of acromegaly.

assertions.text: GH excess causes insidious/slow acral and jaw enlargement.
assertions.quote: Characteristic changes in the face and head, including widening and malocclusion of the jaw and macroglossia, as well as enlarged hands, occur insidiously but are often apparent at initial assessment
assertions.note: Supported by the consensus statement regarding physical examination findings.

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 measurement for typical acral and facial features and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster (sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, debilitating arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis, hypertension).
assertions.note: The Endocrine Society guideline source is provided as an abstract only, which does not contain the specific testing recommendations or listed comorbidity clusters.

units.text: GH-axis drugs commonly cause fluid retention (oedema, arthralgia, paraesthesia, carpal tunnel symptoms), usually transient and dose-related, and glucose intolerance; somatropin labelling asks that pre-existing nevi be monitored for growth or malignant change.

assertions.text: GH-axis drugs commonly cause fluid retention presenting as edema, arthralgia, paresthesia, and carpal tunnel symptoms, which are usually transient and dose-related.
assertions.quote: Clinical manifestations of fluid retention (e.g., edema, arthralgia, myalgia, nerve compression syndromes including carpal tunnel syndrome/paresthesia) are usually transient and dose dependent.
assertions.note: The Genotropin label confirms that clinical manifestations of fluid retention such as edema, arthralgia, paresthesia, and carpal tunnel syndrome are usually transient and dose dependent.

assertions.text: GH-axis drugs can cause glucose intolerance.
assertions.quote: EGRIFTA WR treatment can result in glucose intolerance.
assertions.note: The Egrifta WR label states that treatment can result in glucose intolerance.

assertions.text: Somatropin labelling recommends monitoring preexisting nevi for increased growth or malignant changes.
assertions.quote: Monitor patients on somatropin therapy carefully for increased growth, or potential malignant changes, of preexisting nevi.
assertions.note: The Genotropin prescribing information instructs clinicians to monitor preexisting nevi for growth or malignant change.

units.text: Observed human data on IGF-1 and cancer are associations: higher circulating IGF-1 is linked with modestly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer, with reverse causation not excluded; acromegaly shows a slightly raised cancer incidence in pooled studies (SIR 1.5) that a nationwide cohort did not confirm (SIR 1.1).

assertions.text: Higher circulating IGF-1 is associated with increased risks of prostate, breast, colorectal, and thyroid cancer.
assertions.quote: Higher IGF-I concentration was associated with increased risks of thyroid cancer [HR per 5 nmol/L higher concentration 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.01-1.37] in addition to colorectal (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.03-1.13), breast (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.07-1.15), and prostate cancer (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.05-1.12), and reduced risks of ovarian and liver cancer.
assertions.note: UK Biobank prospective analyses confirmed positive associations between higher IGF-1 and prostate, breast, colorectal, and thyroid cancer.

assertions.text: Reverse causation cannot be excluded as an explanation for the observed associations between IGF-1 and cancer.
assertions.quote: Mean follow-up was 6.9 years and the possibility that the observed associations may be influenced by reverse causality bias cannot be excluded.
assertions.note: The UK Biobank study explicitly states that reverse causality bias cannot be ruled out.

assertions.text: A nationwide cohort study found a standardized incidence ratio (SIR) for cancer of 1.1 in acromegaly patients.
assertions.quote: The cohort study identified 81 cases of cancer after exclusion of cases diagnosed within the first year [SIR 1.1; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.9 to 1.4].
assertions.note: The nationwide cohort study reported an SIR of 1.1 for cancer in acromegaly.

assertions.text: Pooled studies in a meta-analysis showed an overall cancer standardized incidence ratio of 1.5 in acromegaly.
assertions.quote: The meta-analysis yielded an SIR of overall cancer of 1.5 (95% CI, 1.2 to 1.8).
assertions.note: The meta-analysis of 23 studies yielded an overall cancer SIR of 1.5.

units.text: GH treatment cohorts are largely reassuring for replacement: no clear raised cancer risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other major disease, and a 2022 consensus found no association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence; people with GH-receptor deficiency have very little cancer. No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin — the mitogenic risk there is plausible and unmeasured.

assertions.text: A large European cohort of 23,984 GH-treated children showed no clear raised cancer risk in those with growth failure and no other major disease.
assertions.quote: The cohort comprised 23,984 patients treated with recombinant GH (r-hGH) in 8 European countries since this treatment was first used in 1984. Cancer expectations were from country-specific national population statistics. Main Outcome Measures Cancer incidence and cancer mortality. Results Incidence and mortality risks in the cohort were raised for several cancer sites, largely consequent on second primary malignancies in patients given r-hGH after cancer treatment. There was no clear raised risk in patients with growth failure without other major disease.
assertions.note: The SAGhE European cohort study of 23,984 patients found no clear raised cancer risk in patients treated for growth failure without other major disease.

assertions.text: A 2022 consensus statement concluded that current evidence does not support an association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence.
assertions.quote: Current evidence reviewed from the proceedings from the Workshop does not support an association between GH replacement and primary tumour or cancer recurrence.
assertions.note: The 2022 consensus statement confirmed that current evidence does not support an association between GH replacement therapy and primary tumour or cancer recurrence.

assertions.text: Individuals with GH-receptor deficiency have very low rates of cancer.
assertions.quote: The individuals with GHR deficiency (GHRD) exhibited only one non-lethal malignancy and no cases of diabetes, in contrast to 17% cancer and 5% diabetes prevalence in the controls.
assertions.note: Long-term monitoring of GHR-deficient individuals revealed only one non-lethal malignancy compared to a 17% cancer prevalence in unaffected controls.

assertions.text: No long-term cancer safety data exist for GH secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3, making mitogenic risk a biologically plausible but unmeasured concern.
assertions.quote: We summarise structural characteristics, pharmacologic effects, and commonly reported dosing patterns, and we synthesise clinically relevant adverse effects with particular attention to hormonal imbalance, endocrine–metabolic risk, and biologically plausible but unproven mitogenic concerns.
assertions.note: The review documents the complete absence of long-term safety data for these off-label compounds and highlights the biologically plausible, theoretical mitogenic concerns.

units.text: In the UK, somatropin (for example Genotropin) is a prescription-only medicine licensed in children for growth disturbance from growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency, short stature after small-for-gestational-age birth and Prader-Willi syndrome, and in adults for pronounced growth hormone deficiency; somatropin is a Class C controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.

assertions.text: In the UK, somatropin (for example Genotropin) is a prescription-only medicine licensed in children for growth disturbance from growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency, short stature after small-for-gestational-age birth, and Prader-Willi syndrome, and in adults for pronounced growth hormone deficiency.
assertions.quote: Growth disturbance due to insufficient secretion of growth hormone (growth hormone deficiency, GHD) and growth disturbance associated with Turner syndrome or chronic renal insufficiency. Growth disturbance [current height standard deviation score (SDS) < - 2.5 and parental adjusted height SDS < - 1] in short children born small for gestational age (SGA)
assertions.note: Genotropin's UK SmPC confirms its prescription-only status and licensed paediatric and adult indications.

assertions.text: Somatropin is a Class C controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.
assertions.quote: Part III U.K. Class C Drugs 1 U.K. The following substances, namely:— [ F90 (a) ] [ F91 Adinazolam (1-(8-Chloro-6-phenyl-4H-[1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a][1,4]benzodiazepin-1-yl)-N,N-dimethylmethanamine). ] [ F92 Alprazolam. ] [ F93 Amineptine ] [ F94 Aminorex ] [ F95 Bentazepam (5-phenyl-1,3,6,7,8,9-hexahydro-2 H -[1]benzothieno[2,3-e][1,4]diazepin-2-one). ] […] (e) Chorionic Gonadotrophin (HCG). Clenbuterol. Non-human chorionic gonadotrophin. Somatotropin. Somatrem. Somatropin.
assertions.note: Schedule 2, Part III of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 lists Somatropin as a Class C drug.

units.text: A search of MHRA's products database on 25 September 2026 returned no summary of product characteristics, patient leaflet or public assessment report for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin; supplied in the UK, any of them would be an unlicensed medicine, which MHRA guidance reserves for an individual patient's special need that no licensed product meets.

assertions.text: A search of the MHRA's products database on 25 September 2026 returned no summary of product characteristics, patient leaflet, or public assessment report for tesamorelin, sermorelin, or ipamorelin.
assertions.note: The cited database search source is marked UNAVAILABLE and contains no readable text.

assertions.text: MHRA guidance reserves the supply of unlicensed medicines for an individual patient's special need that cannot be met by an equivalent licensed product.
assertions.quote: An unlicensed medicinal product may only be supplied in order to meet the special needs of an individual patient. An unlicensed medicinal product should not be supplied where an equivalent licensed medicinal product can meet the special needs of the patient.
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 confirms that unlicensed medicinal products may only be supplied to meet an individual patient's special needs where a licensed product cannot.

units.text: GRADE rates certainty in four levels (high, moderate, low, very low) for an outcome across a body of evidence, not for a single study or a molecule; randomized trials start high and observational studies start low.

assertions.text: GRADE rates certainty/quality of evidence in four levels (high, moderate, low, very low) applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.quote: GRADE specifies four categories-high, moderate, low, and very low-that are applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.note: Balshem 2011 states that GRADE specifies four categories applied to a body of evidence rather than individual studies.

assertions.text: In GRADE, randomized controlled trials start as high quality/certainty and observational studies start as low quality/certainty.
assertions.quote: Randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence, observational studies as low quality.
assertions.note: Balshem 2011 confirms that randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence and observational studies as low quality.

units.text: Certainty is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (unexplained variability across studies), indirectness (study PICO differs from the question), imprecision (confidence interval crossing the important-difference threshold) and suspected publication bias — which a body of small, industry-funded studies should raise — and can be rated up for large effects.

assertions.text: Certainty of evidence is rated down for inconsistency, which is unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.quote: This third article in a seven part series presents the Core GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach to deciding whether to rate down certainty of evidence due to inconsistency—that is, unexplained variability in results across studies.
assertions.note: The guideline abstract explains rating down for inconsistency due to unexplained variability across studies.

assertions.text: Certainty is rated down for indirectness when the study PICO differs substantially from the target PICO/question.
assertions.quote: When target and study PICOs differ substantially, studies provide indirect evidence and Core GRADE users may rate down the certainty of evidence as a result of this indirectness.
assertions.note: The source notes that when target and study PICOs differ substantially, certainty may be rated down for indirectness.

assertions.text: Certainty is rated down for imprecision when the confidence interval crosses the important-difference threshold (MID).
assertions.quote: Users then rate down for imprecision if the 95% confidence interval crosses the MID for benefit or harm.
assertions.note: The guideline states users rate down for imprecision if the 95% confidence interval crosses the MID for benefit or harm.

assertions.text: A body of small, industry-funded studies should raise suspicion of publication bias.
assertions.quote: For publication bias, a body of evidence comprising small studies funded by industry should raise suspicion.
assertions.note: The guideline directly states that a body of evidence comprising small studies funded by industry raises suspicion of publication bias.

assertions.text: Certainty of evidence can be rated up for large effects.
assertions.quote: Core GRADE users appraising results from well conducted NSRI can consider rating up certainty of evidence when risk ratios from pooled estimates suggest large or very large effects.
assertions.note: The guideline confirms that users can consider rating up certainty when estimates suggest large or very large effects.

units.text: Applied to this course: topical GHK-Cu's only indexed RCT measured post-laser healing (indirect for photoageing); BPC-157 wound data are rodent models (indirect); LL-37's 34-person positive trial and 148-person negative phase IIb disagree (inconsistent); oral collagen's benefit disappears in high-quality trials (risk of bias).

assertions.text: Topical GHK-Cu's only indexed RCT evaluated post-laser healing.
assertions.quote: To evaluate the role of skin care products that contain a copper tripeptide complex, glycyl-l-histidyl-l-lysine-Cu(2+) (GHK-Cu), in treating carbon dioxide (CO(2)) laser-resurfaced skin.
assertions.note: The trial evaluated topical GHK-Cu on laser-resurfaced skin, but the abstract does not confirm it is the only indexed RCT.

assertions.text: BPC-157 wound healing evidence is based on rodent models.
assertions.quote: By simultaneously curing cutaneous and other tissue wounds (colocutaneous, gastrocutaneous, esophagocutaneous, duodenocutaneous, vesicovaginal, and rectovaginal) in rats, the potency of BPC 157 is evident.
assertions.note: The review documents BPC-157 wound-healing data in rat and mouse models.

assertions.text: LL-37 had a positive initial trial with 34 participants.
assertions.quote: This first-in-man trial included 34 participants with VLUs and comprised a 3-week, open-label, run-in period on placebo, followed by a 4-week randomized double-blind treatment phase with twice weekly applications of LL-37 (0.5, 1.6, or 3.2 mg/mL) or placebo, and a 4-week follow-up.
assertions.note: The initial trial enrolled 34 participants and found marked improvements in healing predictors at lower doses.

assertions.text: LL-37's 148-person phase IIb trial was negative in its full study population.
assertions.quote: Efficacy analysis performed on the full study population did not identify any significant improvement in healing in patients treated with LL‐37 as compared with the placebo.
assertions.note: The phase IIb trial in 148 patients did not find significant improvement in healing compared with placebo across the full population.

assertions.text: The apparent benefit of oral collagen supplements disappears in high-quality trials.
assertions.quote: Similarly, high-quality studies revealed no significant effect in all categories, while low-quality studies revealed a significant improvement in elasticity.
assertions.note: High-quality trials in the meta-analysis showed no significant effect across all evaluated skin aging categories.

units.text: A Cochrane methodology review of 75 papers found industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) than non-industry studies, a bias not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessment.

assertions.text: A Cochrane methodology review of 75 papers found that industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) compared to non-industry studies.
assertions.quote: Industry sponsored studies more often had favorable efficacy results, RR: 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) (25 papers) (moderate quality evidence), similar harms results RR: 1.37 (95% CI: 0.64 to 2.93) (four papers) (very low quality evidence) and more often favorable conclusions RR: 1.34 (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.51) (29 papers) (low quality evidence) compared with non-industry sponsored studies.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly reports the 75-paper total, RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.37; moderate quality evidence) for favorable efficacy results, and RR 1.34 for favorable conclusions compared to non-industry studies.

assertions.text: The review found that this industry bias is not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessment.
assertions.quote: Our analyses suggest the existence of an industry bias that cannot be explained by standard 'Risk of bias' assessments.
assertions.note: The review authors conclude that their analyses suggest an industry bias not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessments.

units.text: Both Hormonaly guides attach an A–D letter to the evidence for a specific use — adapted from GRADE's four levels — which rates evidence, not legality; mechanistic appeal never raises a grade, and grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.

assertions.text: Both Hormonaly guides assign an A–D rating adapted from GRADE's four levels to evaluate clinical evidence for a specific use rather than legality.
assertions.quote: Every entry carries a GRADE letter rating derived from the Hormonaly.ai evidence database, which adapts the standard GRADE framework to peptide pharmacology.
assertions.note: The guide confirms it adapts the standard GRADE framework to rate evidence strength for a specific use rather than legality.

assertions.text: Mechanistic appeal never raises an evidence grade.
assertions.quote: Mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly confirms that mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.

assertions.text: Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.
assertions.quote: — Evidence grade and regulatory status are separate checks; clear both.
assertions.note: The text directly states that evidence grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.

units.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and cGMP only if the bulk substance meets a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list — and is made by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis. Quality is defined by reference to those standards and the certificate, not by a numerical purity threshold in the statute's text.

assertions.text: In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use, and cGMP only if the bulk substance complies with a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list.
assertions.note: 21 U.S.C. § 353a and the FDA guidance confirm exemptions and the three-tiered criteria for bulk drug substances.

assertions.text: Bulk drug substances used in 503A compounding must be manufactured by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis.
assertions.quote: In addition, bulk drug substances must be accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis and must have been manufactured by an establishment registered with FDA under section 510 of the FD&C Act.
assertions.note: Both 21 U.S.C. § 353a and the FDA guidance require bulk substances to come from registered establishments with a valid certificate of analysis.

assertions.text: Quality under 503A is defined by reference to monograph standards, FDA approval/listing status, and certificates of analysis rather than a numerical purity threshold in the statutory text.
assertions.quote: (I) comply with the standards of an applicable United States Pharmacopoeia or National Formulary monograph, if a monograph exists, and the United States Pharmacopoeia chapter on pharmacy compounding ; (II) if such a monograph does not exist, are drug substances that are components of drugs approved by the Secretary
assertions.note: The statutory text defines compliance via monograph standards and certificates of analysis without specifying a numerical purity percentage.

units.text: 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, must meet cGMP, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, report adverse events and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions; their products are exempt from approval and adequate-directions requirements, so they remain unapproved.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with the FDA, must comply with cGMP requirements, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, and report adverse events.
assertions.quote:
Outsourcing facilities:

must comply with CGMP requirements;

are inspected by FDA according to a risk-based schedule; and

must meet certain other conditions, such as reporting adverse events and providing FDA with certain information about the products they compound.
assertions.note: FDA guidance details the statutory definition, registration, cGMP compliance, risk-based inspection schedule, and adverse event reporting requirements under Section 503B.

assertions.text: 503B outsourcing facilities may compound drugs without obtaining patient-specific prescriptions.
assertions.quote: An outsourcing facility may or may not obtain prescriptions for identified individual patients.
assertions.note: Section 503B explicitly states that outsourcing facilities may or may not obtain prescriptions for identified individual patients.

assertions.text: Drugs compounded by 503B outsourcing facilities qualify for exemptions from FDA approval and adequate directions for use labeling requirements, remaining unapproved.
assertions.quote: Drugs compounded by an outsourcing facility can qualify for exemptions from FDA approval requirements and the requirement to label products with adequate directions for use, but not from current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements.
assertions.note: The source confirms that drugs compounded by outsourcing facilities can qualify for exemptions from approval and adequate directions for use labeling requirements.

units.text: As of 22 September 2026 the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) holds six substances, none a peptide, unchanged since 2019; listing carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.

assertions.text: As of 2026, the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) contains six substances (none of which is a peptide) and has remained unchanged since 2019.
assertions.quote: A final regulation was issued in February 2019, List of Bulk Drug Substances That Can Be Used To Compound Drug Products in Accordance with Section 503A of the FD&C Act , in which FDA placed six substances on the list, identified and did not place four other substances on the list, and established the criteria to evaluate substances for inclusion on the list.
assertions.note: The FDA regulations page confirms that six substances were placed on the list in the final rule in February 2019.

assertions.text: Inclusion of a substance on the 503A bulks list carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.
assertions.quote: Based on evidence currently available, there are inadequate data to demonstrate the safety or efficacy of any drug product compounded using any of the drug substances listed in paragraph (a) of this section, or to establish general recognition of the safety or effectiveness of any such drug product.
assertions.note: The regulation specifies that there are inadequate data to establish safety or efficacy and that representing products as FDA-endorsed causes them to be misbranded.

units.text: Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, not listing. As of 14 May 2026 Category 1 includes GHK-Cu except injectable routes and 503A Category 2 holds six substances; BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37 and melanotan II sit in a table of withdrawn nominations whose safety concerns remain posted.

assertions.text: Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, rather than final inclusion on the 503A bulks list.
assertions.quote: FDA developed an interim policy describing conditions under which the agency does not intend to take action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities and licensed physicians for compounding drug products from certain bulk drug substances that cannot otherwise be used under section 503A. The agency issued this interim policy to avoid unnecessary disruption to patient treatment while FDA evaluates the bulk drug substances nominated for inclusion on the 503A bulks list .
assertions.note: The FDA explains that categories 1–3 are part of an interim enforcement policy while evaluating nominated bulk drug substances.

assertions.text: As of 14 May 2026, 503A Category 1 includes GHK-Cu except for injectable routes and Category 2 contains six substances.
assertions.quote: GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) will be added back to category 1.
assertions.note: The updated category lists show GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes) added back to Category 1 and exactly six substances in 503A Category 2.

assertions.text: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37, and melanotan II are listed in a table of withdrawn nominations whose safety concerns remain posted.
assertions.quote: This list of bulk drug substances previously in category 2 of the interim policies were withdrawn by the nominators.
assertions.note: The FDA page lists these substances under the table of withdrawn nominations alongside their potential significant safety risks.

units.text: The July 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is advisory; FDA's review staff concluded the listing criteria weigh against BPC-157, and only rulemaking changes the bulks list, which no rule had changed as of September 2026.

assertions.text: The Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is advisory and provides non-binding recommendations to the FDA.
assertions.quote: Advisory committees make non-binding recommendations to the FDA, which generally follows the recommendations but is not legally bound to do so.
assertions.note: The FDA advisory committee calendar states that advisory committees make non-binding recommendations.

assertions.text: FDA's review staff concluded that the evaluation criteria weigh against placing BPC-157 (free base and acetate) on the Section 503A Bulks List.
assertions.quote: For the reasons discussed below, we believe the evaluation criteria weigh against placing both BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate on the list of bulk drug substances that can be used to compound drug products in accordance with section 503A of the FD&C Act (503A Bulks List).
assertions.note: The briefing document concludes that the evaluation criteria weigh against placing BPC-157 on the 503A bulks list.

assertions.text: As of September 2026, no rulemaking had changed 21 CFR 216.23 to include BPC-157 on the list of bulk drug substances that can be used under Section 503A.
assertions.quote: ( a ) The following bulk drug substances can be used in compounding under section 503A(b)(1)(A)(i)(III) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
assertions.note: The regulation text as of September 2026 confirms the codified bulks list has not added BPC-157.

units.text: Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, chemically synthesized or not, so such products are biological products; tesamorelin and hyaluronidase were deemed biologics licences on that date, and biologics are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.

assertions.text: Since March 23, 2020, the FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids (whether chemically synthesized or not), classifying such products as biological products.
assertions.quote: Under this final rule, the term protein means any alpha amino acid polymer with a specific, defined sequence that is greater than 40 amino acids in size.
assertions.note: The final rule effective March 23, 2020 defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer greater than 40 amino acids in size regardless of chemical synthesis.

assertions.text: Tesamorelin and hyaluronidase had their approved NDAs deemed to be biologics licenses (BLAs) on March 23, 2020.
assertions.quote: FDA has provided below a list of each approved application for a biological product under the FD&C Act that was deemed to be a license (i.e., an approved biologics license application (BLA)) for the biological product on March 23, 2020.
assertions.note: Both hyaluronidase and tesamorelin acetate appear on the FDA list of NDAs deemed to be BLAs on March 23, 2020.

assertions.text: Biological products subject to licensure are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions under the FD&C Act.
assertions.quote: This transition affects compounding under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act because, beginning on March 23, these transitioning biological products will not be eligible for the exemptions for compounded drugs under sections 503A and 503B of the FD&C Act.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly notes that biological products subject to licensure under section 351 of the PHS Act are not eligible for 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.

units.text: How residues are counted can decide classification: a federal district court in 2025 upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide (39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain) is not a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question; the appeal was pending as of the latest filings found (June 2026).

assertions.text: In 2025, a federal district court upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide (comprising a 39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain) does not meet the definition of a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question.
assertions.quote: The September 30, 2025 order split: the court upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide does not meet the regulatory definition of a protein, but vacated FDA's separate determination that it could not be "analogous to a protein" and remanded that question to the agency.
assertions.note: The district court order and clinical reference confirm the 2025 ruling upholding the protein determination and remanding the analogous-to-a-protein issue.

assertions.text: The appeal of the district court ruling was pending as of June 2026 filings.
assertions.quote: Lilly appealed in February 2026 (No. 26-1301, 7th Cir.), briefed through June 2026, and the appellate proceeding remains pending as of 13 August 2026.
assertions.note: The appellate docket and case study note show the appeal was briefed through June 2026 and remained pending.

units.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot — mass spectrometry for identity (observed against expected mass), HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results. It cannot establish that the vial in hand is that lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject; lot-less, chromatogram-less, stale (over 12 months) and endotoxin-less certificates are warning signs.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot, evaluating identity by mass spectrometry (observed against expected mass), purity by HPLC, as well as endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal, and solvent results.
assertions.quote: A serious COA tells you what the supplier found on a named lot: whether the mass matches the expected molecule, how pure the material was by HPLC, what counter-ion it carries, and what the endotoxin and microbial results were.
assertions.note: The reference guide details each of these analytical components of a comprehensive Certificate of Analysis.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot establish that the vial in hand is that specific lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The reference source directly lists these limitations of relying solely on a COA.

assertions.text: Certificates of analysis lacking lot numbers, chromatograms, or endotoxin data, or that are over 12 months old, are red flags.
assertions.quote:
— A bare claim of "purity > 99%" with no chromatogram or supporting data.
— No mass spectrum, or a spectrum without a labelled expected mass.
— No batch or lot number; no manufacture date.
— A COA dated more than 12 months before purchase — peptides degrade in storage.
— Generic identical-looking COAs across different products from the same vendor.
— No endotoxin or microbial data on a product marketed for injection.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly lists missing lot numbers, missing chromatograms, lack of endotoxin data, and dates over 12 months old as things that should not be seen on a serious COA.

units.text: There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram: FDA's guidance says the limit is calculated with the USP method from the product's dosage regimen and strength, and some routes (intrathecal, ophthalmic) differ.

assertions.text: There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram.
assertions.quote: There is no single universal per-milligram limit: the allowable endotoxin for a parenteral product is derived from the maximum human dose and the route, so the same concentration can pass for one product and fail for another.
assertions.note: Supported by the clinical reference guide.

assertions.text: FDA guidance states that the endotoxins limit is calculated using USP or AAMI calculation methods.
assertions.quote: The appropriate way to establish the endotoxins limit is to use the calculation methods provided in the USP or AAMI standards.
assertions.note: FDA guidance confirms that endotoxin limits must be established using calculation methods from USP or AAMI standards.

assertions.text: Certain administration routes, such as intrathecal and ophthalmic routes, may have endotoxin limits that differ from standard parenteral calculations.
assertions.quote: Intrathecally-administered products, ophthalmics, or devices (see question 11 for devices) may have endotoxins limits that are not based on the calculation for parenterally administered products.
assertions.note: FDA guidance notes that intrathecally administered products and ophthalmics may have limits not based on standard parenteral calculations.

units.text: FDA's July 2026 briefing on BPC-157 found the nominators' certificates described a different form (the acetate) from the one nominated, that publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits, and that the nominator's certificate mentioned no endotoxin test.

assertions.text: FDA's July 2026 briefing on BPC-157 found that the nominators' certificates described a different form (the acetate) from the one nominated.
