assertions.quote: Due to inconsistencies in the nomination packages, the nominated BDS is unclear from both nominators of BPC-157-related BDSs. For example, the nominated BDS is not consistent with what is listed in the Certificate of Analysis (CoA).
assertions.note: The FDA briefing document notes that the nominated bulk drug substance was inconsistent with the certificates of analysis provided (which were for the acetate form).

assertions.text: Publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits.
assertions.quote: We conducted literature searches and found that most CoAs for BPC-157 (free base) only contain purity testing results, an example of which is shown below (Figure 2). 17 There is no information about the impurity limits/testing results in the CoA to demonstrate control of the impurity profile of BPC- 157 (free base).
assertions.note: The FDA's literature searches showed that most publicly available CoAs only reported purity testing without impurity limits.

assertions.text: The nominator's certificate mentioned no endotoxin test.
assertions.quote: No bioburden/endotoxin test is mentioned in the CoA provided by the nominator. Endotoxin test is considered a critical quality attribute to control microbiological quality of a BDS intended for an injection product.
assertions.note: The briefing explicitly notes that no bioburden or endotoxin test was mentioned in the CoA submitted by the nominator.

units.text: Paperwork and contents can diverge: three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label, 29–39% more peptide than labelled and endotoxin in every vial; a seized injection vial held an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Neither study concerns skin peptides.

assertions.text: Three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label and 29–39% more peptide than labelled.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, the measured semaglutide purity was significantly low, ranging between 7.7% and 14.37% and deviating from the 99% claimed on product labels by manufacturers.
assertions.note: Ashraf et al. found purity between 7.7% and 14.37% (vs. 99% labeled) and semaglutide amounts exceeding labeled amounts by 28.56%–38.69%.

assertions.text: Endotoxin was detected in all three purchased semaglutide vials.
assertions.quote: The lyophilized peptide samples were devoid of viable microorganisms at the time of testing; however, endotoxin was detected in all samples with levels ranging between 2.1645 EU/mg and 8.9511 EU/mg.
assertions.note: Ashraf et al. detected bacterial endotoxin in all delivered peptide samples.

assertions.text: A seized injection vial contained an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable by high-resolution mass spectrometry.
assertions.quote: Therefore, in the present work, a qualitative analysis by liquid chromatography coupled to high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry with a quadrupole time-of-flight analyzer was performed to identify a new heptapeptide (MW = 874.02 Da) - a glycine analogue of GHRP-2.
assertions.note: Popławska et al. identified a novel glycine analogue of GHRP-2 in a seized injection vial using high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry.

units.text: 'Not for use in humans' research labelling (21 CFR 312.160) permits shipment only for laboratory or in-vitro research, and FDA reads intended use objectively from claims, advertising and the circumstances of distribution (21 CFR 201.128); a research-use-only product therefore has no clinical route, and a certificate does not create one.

assertions.text: Under 21 CFR 312.160, labeling a drug with 'Not for use in humans' authorizes shipment solely for tests in vitro or laboratory research animals.
assertions.quote:
A person may ship a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or in animals used only for laboratory research purposes if it is labeled as follows:

CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 authorizes shipment of a drug intended solely for tests in vitro or laboratory research animals when labeled with this cautionary text.

assertions.text: Under 21 CFR 201.128, intended use refers to objective intent, which may be shown by labeling claims, advertising, statements, and the circumstances surrounding distribution.
assertions.quote: The intent may be shown by such persons' expressions, the design or composition of the article, or by the circumstances surrounding the distribution of the article. This objective intent may, for example, be shown by labeling claims, advertising matter, or oral or written statements by such persons or their representatives.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 201.128 defines intended uses as objective intent demonstrated through labeling claims, advertising, and distribution circumstances.

assertions.text: A research-use-only (RUO) product provides no lawful clinical pathway or route for patient administration.
assertions.quote:
Research-use-only (RUO)
Labeled "not for human use"; no GMP/QC guarantee ·
Not a clinical route; impurity, dose, and
contamination risk.
assertions.note: The pocket guide confirms that research-use-only material is not a clinical pathway or lawful route.

units.text: In the US the regime follows intended use and route: appearance claims make a cosmetic (no premarket approval), while a claim to affect structure or function — such as 'regenerate cells' — makes a drug, and 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning; dietary supplements are not approved before sale, their makers being responsible for safety and labelling.

assertions.text: In the US, appearance claims establish a product as a cosmetic, which does not require FDA premarket approval.
assertions.quote: Under the FD&C Act, cosmetic products and ingredients, with the exception of color additives, do not require FDA approval before they go on the market.
assertions.note: FDA guidance specifies that cosmetics (intended for altering appearance or promoting attractiveness) do not require premarket approval.

assertions.text: A claim to affect bodily structure or function, such as 'regenerate cells', classifies a product as a drug under US law.
assertions.quote: Such claims establish the product as a drug because the intended use is to treat or prevent disease or otherwise affect the structure or functions of the human body. Some examples are claims that products will restore hair growth, reduce cellulite, treat varicose veins, increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin, or regenerate cells.
assertions.note: FDA explicitly lists claims to affect bodily structure/function, including cell regeneration, as establishing a product as a drug.

assertions.text: The term 'cosmeceutical' has no meaning or recognition under US law.
assertions.quote: The FD&C Act does not recognize any such category as "cosmeceuticals." A product can be a drug, a cosmetic, or a combination of both, but the term "cosmeceutical" has no meaning under the law.
assertions.note: The FD&C Act does not recognize cosmeceuticals, and the term has no statutory meaning.

assertions.text: Dietary supplements are not approved before marketing, and their makers/distributors are responsible for ensuring safety and proper labelling.
assertions.quote: That means that these firms are responsible for evaluating the safety and labeling of their products before marketing to ensure that they meet all the requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as amended by DSHEA and FDA regulations.
assertions.note: FDA notes that under DSHEA, supplement firms must evaluate safety and labeling prior to marketing.

units.text: 'Off-label' describes unapproved use of an approved drug; a never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy that its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products did not qualify for the 503A exemptions.

assertions.text: 'Off-label' describes unapproved use of an FDA-approved drug, such that a never-approved peptide has no label to depart from.
assertions.quote: Off-label prescribing presupposes an approved product to be off the label of; for a never-approved peptide the marketing prohibition is unrelieved and the adequate-directions exemption is unavailable.
assertions.note: FDA guidance and the clinical reference confirm that off-label use applies to approved drugs, whereas never-approved peptides have no approved labeling.

assertions.text: Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act.
assertions.quote: Under sections 505(a) and 301(d) of the FDCA [21 U.S.C. § 331(d)], a new drug may not be introduced into or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce unless an application approved by FDA under section 505 of the FDCA is in effect for the drug.
assertions.note: The FDA warning letter cites the FD&C Act provisions prohibiting the introduction of unapproved new drugs into interstate commerce.

assertions.text: FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy that its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products did not qualify for Section 503A exemptions.
assertions.quote: For example, the investigators noted that your firm compounded drug products using Follistatin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Endurobal, AOD 9604, BPC 157, Bremelanotide (PT-141), Cerebrolysin, DSIP, Epitalon, GHK-Cu, IGF1-LR3, Ipamorelin, LL-37, Melanotan II, PEG-MGF, Selank, Semax, CJC 1295, SARMS, LGD-4033, and MK 677.
assertions.note: The FDA warning letter to Tailor Made Compounding specifically identifies BPC 157 and GHK-Cu among bulk substances failing to qualify for 503A exemptions.

units.text: For an unapproved or compounded peptide the chart should name the article and its regulatory status in those terms; if compounded, the pathway, facility and certificate relied on; consent covering non-approval, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives (including doing nothing) and what happens if harm occurs — elements the Peptide Pocket Guide borrows from FDA's research-consent rule; the evidence grade quoted; monitoring and a stopping rule; and the date the FDA lists were checked.

assertions.text: For an unapproved or compounded peptide, charting should document the article and its regulatory status in those terms, and if compounded, record the pathway, facility, and certificate of analysis relied on.
assertions.quote: 1. Document the identity of the article and its regulatory status in the chart, in those terms — not as off-label use of an approved drug. 2. Where a compounded preparation is used, record the pathway (503A or 503B), the facility, and the certificate of analysis relied on.
assertions.note: The guide instructs clinicians to document the identity and regulatory status in the chart and record the compounding pathway, facility, and certificate of analysis.

assertions.text: Consent documentation should cover non-approval, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives (including doing nothing), and available care if injury occurs, elements borrowed from the FDA research-consent rule.
assertions.quote: 3. Build consent around the elements FDA's research-consent regulation enumerates: that the therapy is not approved for the indication, the foreseeable risks, the approved alternatives, and what is available if injury occurs.
assertions.note: The guide specifies building consent around FDA research-consent elements, covering lack of approval, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives, and available remedies if injury occurs.

assertions.text: Documentation should include the evidence grade, monitoring and stopping rules, and verification of FDA category/listing status.
assertions.quote: Document the following: — GRADE of evidence — Regulatory status — Alternatives offered — Expected effects — Monitoring plan — Discontinuation criteria
assertions.note: The guide recommends recording the evidence GRADE, monitoring plan, discontinuation criteria, and verifying FDA listing status at prescribing.

units.text: In the UK, regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 lifts the marketing-authorisation requirement (regulation 46) for a 'special' supplied in response to an unsolicited order, manufactured to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under that person's direct responsibility, to meet the patient's special needs; no advertisement may be published, and UK manufacture requires a manufacturer's licence for special medicinal products.

assertions.text: In the UK, regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 lifts the marketing-authorisation requirement (regulation 46) for a 'special' supplied in response to an unsolicited order, manufactured to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under that person's direct responsibility, to meet the patient's special needs.
assertions.note: Regulation 167(1) explicitly provides this exemption from regulation 46 under these exact conditions.

assertions.text: Under regulation 167, no advertisement relating to the special medicinal product may be published.
assertions.quote: (3) Condition B is that no advertisement relating to the medicinal product is published by any person.
assertions.note: Condition B of regulation 167 prohibits publishing any advertisement relating to the product.

assertions.text: UK manufacture of special medicinal products requires a manufacturer's licence for special medicinal products.
assertions.quote: 4.1  The manufacturer or assembler of “specials” must hold a Manufacturer’s “Specials” Licence granted by the Licensing Authority.
assertions.note: The regulations and MHRA guidance state that UK manufacture of specials requires a Manufacturer's Specials Licence.

units.text: MHRA Guidance Note 14: specials are made in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy; an unlicensed product should not be supplied where a licensed product can meet the patient's special need, and special need excludes cost, convenience and operational reasons; the order of preference is a UK-licensed product (even off-label), then a product licensed in its country of origin, then a UK special, with products that are not medicines in their country of origin, such as supplements, least acceptable.

assertions.text: Under MHRA Guidance Note 14, specials are made in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed for quality, safety, and efficacy.
assertions.quote: If none of these options will suffice, then a completely unlicensed product may have to be used, for example, UK manufactured "specials", which are made in GMP inspected facilities, but which are otherwise un-assessed (GMP inspection of “specials” manufacturers is not product specific).
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 confirms specials are manufactured in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed.

assertions.text: An unlicensed product should not be supplied where a licensed product can meet the patient's special clinical need, and special need excludes cost, convenience, and operational reasons.
assertions.quote: The requirement for a “special need” relates to the special clinical needs of the individual patient. It does not include reasons of cost, convenience or operational needs (see Section 10 of this guide).
assertions.note: The guidance explicitly prohibits supplying an unlicensed product when a licensed alternative suffices and states special need excludes cost, convenience, or operational needs.

assertions.text: The hierarchy of preference is a UK-licensed product (even off-label), followed by a product licensed in its country of origin, then a UK special, with products not classed as medicines in their country of origin (such as supplements) being least acceptable.
assertions.quote: The least acceptable products are those that are unlicensed in the country of origin, and which are not classed as medicines in the country of origin (but are in the UK). For example, the use of products from countries where they are classed as supplements, not pharmaceuticals, and may not be made to expected standards of pharmaceutical GMP. These should be avoided whenever possible.
assertions.note: Appendix 2 outlines this exact 5-level hierarchy of preference.

units.text: A pharmacist may also prepare or dispense a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy, hospital or health centre in accordance with a prescription without a marketing authorisation (Medicines Act 1968, s. 10); MHRA counts such pharmacy preparations among unlicensed medicines.

assertions.text: Under section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968, a pharmacist may prepare or dispense a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy, hospital, or health centre in accordance with a prescription without a marketing authorisation.
assertions.quote:
The restrictions imposed by [ F2 regulations 17(1) (manufacturing of medicinal products) and 46 (requirement for authorisation) of the 2012 Regulations ] do not apply to anything which is done in a registered pharmacy, a hospital [ F3 , a care home service ] or a health centre and is done there by or under the supervision of a pharmacist and consists of— 

(a) preparing or dispensing a medicinal product in accordance with a prescription given by [ F4 an appropriate practitioner ]
assertions.note: Section 10(1) exempts pharmacy preparation and dispensing in accordance with a prescription from the marketing authorisation requirement (regulation 46).

assertions.text: MHRA treats medicinal products prepared in a pharmacy under section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968 as unlicensed medicinal products.
assertions.quote: A holder of a Manufacturer’s “Specials” Licence may also be a registered pharmacy supplying unlicensed medicinal products prepared under the exemption provided by section 10 of the 1968 Medicines Act and regulation 4 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012.
assertions.note: The MHRA guidance document expressly lists products prepared under section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968 as unlicensed medicinal products.

units.text: UK professional guidance puts responsibility for an unlicensed medicine on its prescriber: GMC — be satisfied there is sufficient evidence or experience of safety and efficacy, take responsibility for prescribing and for overseeing care and follow-up, record the reasons when not following common practice, and explain to the patient when the use is not routine or licensed alternatives exist; MHRA advises the same and names doctors, dentists, independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers as able to prescribe unlicensed medicines; the GPhC asks pharmacist prescribers to be sure of sufficient evidence and to record discussions and reasons; the NMC Code limits prescribing to the registrant's training, competence, the law and guidance.

assertions.text: GMC guidance requires prescribers of unlicensed medicines to be satisfied there is sufficient evidence or experience of safety and efficacy, take responsibility for prescribing and overseeing care/follow-up, record reasons when not following common practice, and explain to the patient when use is not routine or licensed alternatives exist.
assertions.quote:
be satisfied that there is a sufficient evidence base and/or experience of using the medicine to show its safety and efficacy

take responsibility for prescribing the medicine and for overseeing the patient’s care, including monitoring and follow-up

record the medicine prescribed and, where common practice is not being followed, the reasons for prescribing this medicine
assertions.note: MHRA advice for prescribers (citing GMC guidance) confirms the requirements for evidence of safety/efficacy, responsibility for care and follow-up, and recording reasons when common practice is not followed.

recheck.note: MHRA advice for prescribers (citing GMC guidance) confirms the requirements for evidence of safety/efficacy, responsibility for care and follow-up, and recording reasons when common practice is not followed.

assertions.text: MHRA advises the same prescribing principles and names doctors, dentists, independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers as able to prescribe unlicensed medicines.
assertions.quote: At present, the following healthcare professionals can prescribe an unlicensed medicine: doctors; dentists; independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers (who can be a pharmacist, nurse, midwife, community nurse, optometrist, physiotherapist, radiographer, or chiropodist/podiatrist).
assertions.note: MHRA lists these exact healthcare professional groups and prescribing responsibilities.

assertions.text: The GPhC requires pharmacist prescribers to be sure of sufficient evidence/experience and to record discussions and reasons when prescribing unlicensed medicines.
assertions.quote: in the case of an unlicensed or ‘off-label’ medicine, make sure there is sufficient evidence and experience of its safety and effectiveness, and of the appropriateness of its use to meet the needs of the person.
assertions.note: The GPhC guidance explicitly requires sufficient evidence and experience of safety and effectiveness, as well as recording discussions and reasons.

assertions.text: The NMC Code limits prescribing to the registrant's training, competence, the law, and relevant guidance/regulations.
assertions.quote: 18 Advise on, prescribe, supply, dispense or administer medicines within the limits of your training and competence, the law, our guidance and other relevant policies, guidance and regulations
assertions.note: Standard 18 of the NMC Code explicitly states this limitation.

units.text: In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicinal product from all its claims (including websites and social media), its presentation, its product form (such as injection) and the way it is used; a medicinal product with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or offered for sale (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, reg. 46) or advertised (reg. 279).

assertions.text: In the UK, the MHRA determines whether a product is a medicinal product based on factors including all its claims (including websites and social media), its presentation, its product form (such as injection), and the way it is used.
assertions.quote: The MHRA considers the following factors: • all claims made for the product, both explicit and implicit, including any made on websites, linked helplines, testimonials, linked publications, or in social media. Implicit claims may include product names • the context in which the claims are made, and the overall presentation
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 8 specifies that MHRA considers all claims (including on websites and social media), context and presentation, product form (capsule, tablet, injection, etc.), and the way it is to be used.

assertions.text: Under regulation 46 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012, an unauthorised medicinal product may not be sold, supplied, or offered for sale or supply.
assertions.quote: 46. —(1) A person may not sell or supply, or offer to sell or supply, an unauthorised medicinal product.
assertions.note: Regulation 46(1) provides that a person may not sell or supply, or offer to sell or supply, an unauthorised medicinal product.

assertions.text: Under regulation 279 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012, a medicinal product without appropriate UK marketing authorisation or registration may not be advertised.
assertions.quote: 279. — (1) A person may not publish an advertisement in Great Britain for a medicinal product unless one of the following is in force for the product— (a) a UKMA(GB) or UKMA(UK);
assertions.note: Regulation 279 prohibits publishing an advertisement for a medicinal product unless an appropriate authorisation or registration is in force.

units.text: MHRA classifies injectable melanotan products as medicines and has removed melanotan products from the market (FOI 24/274, April 2024); its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, on 28 May 2026, included peptide products.

assertions.text: The MHRA classifies injectable melanotan products as medicines.
assertions.quote: Products containing Melanotan II are classified as medicines if they are injectable or pens.
assertions.note: Supported by the MHRA FOI response explaining classification of injectable melanotan products.

assertions.text: The MHRA has taken action to remove melanotan products from the market.
assertions.quote: However, the MHRA has repeatedly taken action to remove Melanotan products from the market for over 10 years and will continue to do so where products fall within the definition of a medicinal product
assertions.note: Supported by the FOI response noting recurring enforcement actions against melanotan products.

assertions.text: The MHRA's largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines occurred on 28 May 2026 and included peptide products.
assertions.quote: The property is believed to have been used as a large-scale facility to manufacture, assemble, and distribute unlicensed weight loss medicines, including retatrutide and tirzepatide, as well as peptide products.
assertions.note: Supported by the press release detailing the 28 May 2026 raid involving weight-loss medicines and peptide products.

units.text: UK law prohibits publishing an advertisement likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine (reg. 284), and CAP Code rule 12.12 bars advertising prescription-only medicines to the public; MHRA's Blue Guide lets clinics promote a service such as 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' provided they do not name a prescription-only medicine, and says unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned.

assertions.text: UK law prohibits publishing an advertisement likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine under regulation 284 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012.
assertions.quote: 284. —(1) A person may not publish an advertisement that is likely to lead to the use of a prescription only medicine.
assertions.note: Regulation 284(1) of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 expressly prohibits publishing an advertisement likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine.

assertions.text: CAP Code rule 12.12 bars advertising prescription-only medicines to the public.
assertions.quote: Prescription-only medicines or prescription-only medical treatments may not be advertised to the public.
assertions.note: Rule 12.12 of the CAP Code states that prescription-only medicines or medical treatments may not be advertised to the public.

assertions.text: The MHRA Blue Guide allows clinics to promote a service such as 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' provided they do not name a prescription-only medicine.
assertions.quote: As an example, advertising for cosmetic clinics and beauty salons may promote the service provided, e.g. “treat ment for lines and wrinkles”, as this is non-specific and may include various procedures.   Advertising mate rials such as magazine advertisements and flyers distributed to the public mu st not mention product names such as “Botox” or “botulinum toxin”.
assertions.note: The Blue Guide states that clinics may promote non-specific services like 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' but must not mention product names such as Botox.

assertions.text: The MHRA Blue Guide states that unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned.
assertions.quote: Unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned, to comply with re gulation 279 of the Regulations which prohibi ts advertising of medicines for  w h i c h  n o  marketing authorisation or regist ration is in force.
assertions.note: The Blue Guide confirms that unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned in accordance with regulation 279.

units.text: On 11 February 2026 the ASA upheld a complaint that Instagram posts by customers of an online pharmacy's referral scheme, carrying discount codes and hashtags such as '#mounjaro', promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public.

assertions.text: On 11 February 2026, the ASA upheld a complaint that Instagram posts by participants in an online pharmacy's referral scheme, which included discount codes and hashtags such as '#mounjaro', promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public.
assertions.quote: We therefore considered the references to “mounjaro” in the ads, whether or not such references were preceded by a hashtag or were part of larger references such as “mounjarojourney”, “mounjaroweightlossjourney”, “mounjarotribe” or “voymounjaro”, promoted POMs to the public.
assertions.note: The ASA ruling published on 11 February 2026 confirmed that referral scheme posts containing discount codes and hashtags referencing Mounjaro promoted prescription-only medicines to the public in breach of the CAP Code.

units.text: GMC guidance for doctors who offer cosmetic interventions requires a physical examination before prescribing injectable cosmetic medicines, which therefore may not be prescribed by telephone, video link or online for patients the doctor has not examined.
units.note: no cited source has readable text — nothing can be verified

units.text:
The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages · three lessons
Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.
Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 01
The skin makes its own hormones.
This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.
1.2 Receptor maps: what a cell atlas can and cannot show
Set your path
How will you use this course?
The evidence, grades and regulatory facts are the same for everyone. What changes, in every module, is the 'what you do …

assertions.text: The skin makes its own hormones.
assertions.quote: Hormones influence the development and function of human skin which also produces and releases hormones.
assertions.note: Zouboulis (2004) confirms that human skin synthesizes and releases its own hormones.

units.text:
Lesson 1.1 · Concept
Four units, one circuit.
Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.
Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work
Narration: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts…
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

assertions.text: The skin is described as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ structured into four regulatory units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal (hair follicles and glands).
assertions.quote: This skin neuro-immuno-endocrine system is compartmentalized through the formation of epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal regulatory units.
assertions.note: Slominski (2025) confirms the skin neuro-immuno-endocrine system is organized into epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal units.

assertions.text: Each unit contains resident cells capable of producing hormones and mounting immune responses, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, adipocytes, and mast cells.
assertions.quote: Each contains resident cells with both hormone-making and immune capacity (keratinocytes, melanocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, adipocytes, mast cells, dendritic and Langerhans cells), wired together by sensory nerves that penetrate to the stratum corneum.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) specifies that each unit contains resident cells with hormone-making and immune capacities.

assertions.text: Skin signaling operates across three main pathways: local paracrine signaling between neighbouring cells, neural transmission via sensory nerves, and systemic endocrine transmission through the bloodstream.
assertions.quote: Communication runs three ways: soluble factors between neighboring cells, rapid neural transmission, and release into the circulation that can reach distant organs.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) states that cutaneous communication runs via soluble factors between neighboring cells, neural transmission, and circulation to distant organs.

assertions.text: The mechanistic understanding of cutaneous neuro-immuno-endocrinology is largely derived from experimental work across cell types, tissues, and animal species.
assertions.quote: This is not a fringe idea — the hypothesis that the skin is a self-contained neuroendocrine organ, articulated decades ago, has since been validated experimentally across cell types and species.[3]
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) notes that the concept of cutaneous neuroendocrinology has been validated experimentally across cell types and species.

units.text:
Mechanism
A steroid factory with local axes.
Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.
Steroid synthesis
Cholesterol to cortisol, androgens and estrogens
CYP11A1 starts the chain; 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase activate precursors from the blood. Cell and tissue studies.
HPA-like loop
CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with feedback
Human scalp follicles kept alive in culture. Ex vivo, human tissue.
Keratinocyte glucocorticoids
Set local immune tone
Genetic deletion in mouse keratinocytes. Animal evidence.
Thyroid-like loop
TRH, TSH and deiodinases → T3
Keratinocyte growth and the hair cycle. Mostly mouse models.
Somatotropic loop
GH and …
units.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

assertions.text: Skin cells possess the enzymes to synthesize steroids de novo from cholesterol or activate precursors from the bloodstream, functioning as shortened local equivalents of central hormone axes.
assertions.quote: Most recently it has been established that skin cells contain the entire biochemical apparatus necessary for production of glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens either from precursors of systemic origin or, alternatively, through the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone and its subsequent transformation to biologically active steroids.
assertions.note: Slominski (2013) notes that skin cells contain the biochemical machinery to generate glucocorticoids, androgens, and estrogens from cholesterol or systemic precursors.

assertions.text: CYP11A1 initiates steroidogenesis from cholesterol, while enzymes such as 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, and aromatase activate systemic or local precursors.
assertions.quote: Skin cells express CYP11A1, the rate-limiting enzyme that cleaves cholesterol to pregnenolone, and can build glucocorticoids, androgens, and estrogens locally — or activate precursors delivered from the blood. Local interconversion uses familiar enzymes: 11β-HSD1/2 for cortisol, 5α-reductase for dihydrotestosterone, and 17β-HSD for sex-steroid steps.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) summarizes that skin cells express CYP11A1 to initiate steroidogenesis alongside 11β-HSD, 5α-reductase, and aromatase.

assertions.text: Organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles operate a local HPA-like loop (CRH → ACTH → cortisol) complete with regulatory feedback.
assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.
assertions.note: Ito et al. (2005) showed that cultured human scalp hair follicles express a functional HPA equivalent responding to CRH with ACTH and cortisol production, and undergo negative feedback.

assertions.text: Keratinocyte-derived de novo glucocorticoids set local immune tone, as demonstrated by genetic knockout models in mice.
assertions.quote: Our study thus emphasizes the important immunoregulatory role of skin-derived GC in the regulation of the cutaneous immune system and provides mechanistic insight on the critical role of skin GC in maintaining homeostasis under physiological conditions and in different prevalent inflammatory skin diseases.
assertions.note: Phan et al. (2021) demonstrated using keratinocyte-specific Cyp11b1 knockout mice that endogenous keratinocyte glucocorticoids regulate skin immune homeostasis.

assertions.text: The skin contains a thyroid-like loop (TRH, TSH, deiodinases generating T3) that influences keratinocyte growth and hair cycling, evidenced largely in mouse models.
assertions.quote: In the past 2 decades, in vivo analysis of mouse models of TH deregulation has contributed clarifying some aspects of the molecular mechanisms regulated by TH in keratinocytes. Although promising results have been obtained indicating how the modulation of TH signal can affect keratinocyte proliferation/differentiation balance and therefore influence pathophysiological mechanisms such as wound healing and hair follicle cycle
assertions.note: Mancino et al. (2021) review the presence of TRH/TSH receptors and deiodinases in skin and their effects on keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation, and hair follicle cycling in mouse models.

assertions.text: Human hair follicles operate a somatotropic loop (GH and IGF-1) ex vivo.
assertions.quote: The human hair follicle runs functional peripheral equivalents of the central axes: it synthesizes cortisol and operates a local HPA-like loop,[11] and ex vivo it sustains a hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent (GHRH, GH, IGF-1) that paces its own growth.[12]
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) describes that human hair follicles sustain an ex vivo hypothalamic–pituitary–somatotropic equivalent pacing hair growth.

assertions.text: POMC is cleaved in skin into α-MSH, ACTH, and β-endorphin, regulating pigmentation, barrier function, and local immune restraint.
assertions.quote: The skin makes and processes POMC into ACTH, α-MSH, and β-endorphin, acting on melanocortin receptors MC1–MC5 to govern pigment, barrier strength, sebum, and local immunosuppression.[8]
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) describes the skin's processing of POMC into these peptides and their roles in pigment, barrier strength, and immunosuppression.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide characterizes local axis biology as mechanistic foundation rather than a dosing rationale.
assertions.quote:
Read as foundation
much of the local-steroidogenesis literature is
mechanistic (cell and ex-vivo); it explains biology, but
is not a dosing rationale.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni (2026) specifically notes that local steroidogenesis literature explains biology but does not serve as a dosing rationale.

assertions.text: Keratinocytes synthesize cortisol locally to restrain cutaneous immune cells (local loop).
assertions.quote: Keratinocytes control tissue homeostasis and skin inflammation via immunosuppressive glucocorticoids.
assertions.note: Keratinocyte-derived glucocorticoids autonomously regulate local immune tone and inflammation.

assertions.text: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3 in the skin, which enters the circulation and travels to the liver (skin to body).
assertions.quote: D3 is produced in the skin from 7-DHC in a nonenzymatic process in which the B ring is broken by UVB radiation, and the pre-D3 formed isomerizes to D3 in a thermo-sensitive process. D3 is converted to 25OHD3 in the liver and elsewhere by a number of enzymes of which CYP2R1 is the most important.
assertions.note: Vitamin D3 synthesized in the skin under UVB enters the bloodstream to undergo hepatic 25-hydroxylation.

assertions.text: Cushing syndrome causes cutaneous manifestations including violaceous striae, thin skin, and easy bruising (body to skin).
assertions.quote: The genuine endocrine entity is the moon facies of Cushing’s syndrome — a rounded, plethoric face with dorsocervical and supraclavicular fat pads, central adiposity, wide purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, and easy bruising — a referable diagnosis, not a cosmetic state.
assertions.note: Systemic hypercortisolism in Cushing syndrome manifests with characteristic skin changes including purple striae and bruising.

assertions.text: Cultured scalp hair follicles secrete cortisol and exhibit negative feedback on their own CRH expression (local loop).
assertions.quote: Finally, human hair follicles display HPA axis-like regulatory feedback systems, since the glucocorticoid receptor agonist hydrocortisone down-regulates follicular CRH expression.
assertions.note: Hair follicles operate an autonomous HPA-like loop that synthesizes cortisol and down-regulates follicular CRH.

assertions.text: Skin converts circulating precursors into active androgens and estrogens that contribute to systemic hormone levels (skin to body).
assertions.quote: The cutaneous steroidogenic system can also have systemic effects, which are emphasized by significant skin contribution to circulating androgens and/or estrogens.
assertions.note: Cutaneous steroidogenesis converts precursors into sex steroids that contribute significantly to systemic circulating pools.

assertions.text: Hypothyroidism causes dry, coarse skin and myxedema (body to skin).
assertions.quote: Hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse, cool skin and myxedema; hyperthyroidism gives warm, moist skin and, in Graves' disease, pretibial myxedema.[8]
assertions.note: Systemic thyroid hormone deficiency causes coarsened, dry skin and dermal myxedema.

assertions.text: Scalp hair follicles locally convert testosterone to DHT, causing miniaturization of susceptible follicles (local loop).
assertions.quote: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which paradoxically miniaturizes genetically susceptible scalp follicles (androgenetic alopecia) while driving beard and body hair.
assertions.note: Local 5α-reductase activity in hair follicles produces DHT, driving follicle miniaturization in androgenetic alopecia.

Which direction?
One finding at a time: which way does the signal run?
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "Keratinocytes make cortisol that restrains immune cells in the same patch of skin" → Local loop
Explanation: Local loop. Made and used where it is produced; the functional proof comes from mice that cannot make it in keratinocytes and develop skin inflammation.
Sorting item (the learner sorts this statement; the course's claim is only the category): "UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3, which the blood carries to the liver" → Skin to body
Explanation: Skin to body. Vitamin D3 made in the skin is released into the circulation and activated elsewhere. Established human physiology.

assertions.text: Mice with keratinocyte-specific deficiency in de novo glucocorticoid synthesis develop spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.quote: genetic in vivo Cyp11b1 ablation and long-term GC deficiency in keratinocytes primed the murine skin immune system resulting in spontaneous skin inflammation.
assertions.note: The study demonstrated that keratinocyte-specific Cyp11b1 ablation led to spontaneous skin inflammation in mice.

assertions.text: Vitamin D3 synthesized in the skin is translocated into the general circulation.
assertions.quote: The vitamin D-binding protein preferentially translocates the thermal product, vitamin D3, into the circulation.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that vitamin D binding protein translocates synthesized vitamin D3 from skin into the circulation.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide identifies suspected Cushing syndrome as an indication for prompt referral.
assertions.quote: Distinguish the lifestyle-and-fluid “cortisol face” from the moon facies of Cushing’s syndrome — screen red flags (purple striae, proximal myopathy, bruising) and refer.
assertions.note: The guide specifically lists suspected Cushing syndrome with features such as violaceous striae under prompt referral recommendations.

assertions.text: Cultured human scalp hair follicles secrete cortisol and downregulate CRH expression in response to glucocorticoids.
assertions.quote: Finally, human hair follicles display HPA axis-like regulatory feedback systems, since the glucocorticoid receptor agonist hydrocortisone down-regulates follicular CRH expression.
assertions.note: Organ-cultured human scalp hair follicles secreted cortisol and exhibited negative feedback on CRH expression.

assertions.text: Skin converts circulating precursors into sex steroids that contribute to circulating levels, particularly in older adults.
assertions.quote: The skin-located formation of E1 from circulating androstenedione can be the main site of estrogen biosynthesis in postmenopausal women, obese individuals and elderly men.
assertions.note: The review states that skin conversion of circulating precursors forms estrone and contributes significantly in postmenopausal and elderly individuals.

assertions.text: Hypothyroidism causes myxedema via dermal acid mucopolysaccharide/glycosaminoglycan accumulation.
assertions.quote: The name “myxedema” refers to the associated skin condition caused by increased glycosaminoglycan deposition in the skin. Generalized myxedema is still the classic cutaneous sign of hypothyroidism.
assertions.note: The source explains that myxedema in hypothyroidism is caused by glycosaminoglycan accumulation in the skin.

assertions.text: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT in the pilosebaceous unit, serving as the driver/substrate of acne, androgenetic alopecia, and hirsutism.
assertions.quote: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT in the pilosebaceous unit — the substrate of acne, androgenetic alopecia, and hirsutism.
assertions.note: The guide directly states that 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT in the pilosebaceous unit as the substrate of these conditions.

units.text:
What changes in practice
Read the skin before the serum.
The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.
A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment
Narration: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the who…
units.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5 clinical pearl and referral list · Safer 2011

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide notes that sudden skin thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess, coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism, and new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance.
assertions.quote: Sudden skin thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance; rapid photoaging tracks UV, glycation, and smoking.
assertions.note: The guide outlines these specific skin manifestations as indicators of systemic endocrine conditions.

assertions.text: The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.
assertions.quote:
REFER TO ENDOCRINOLOGY PROMPTLY IF
— Suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes).
— Rapidly progressive virilization (deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapid hirsutism) — possible androgen-secreting tumor.
assertions.note: The guide's referral criteria include suspected Cushing syndrome and rapidly progressive virilization.

assertions.text: The guide emphasizes that local cutaneous steroidogenesis and skin biology explain physiological mechanisms but do not justify dosing patients with hormones.
assertions.quote: much of the local-steroidogenesis literature is mechanistic (cell and ex-vivo); it explains biology, but is not a dosing rationale.
assertions.note: The guide explicitly notes that local steroidogenesis literature explains biology but provides no rationale for dosing.

units.text:
Fictional case. A 52-year-old has new thin, easily bruised skin on her forearms, new violaceous striae and newly raised blood pressure. She has read that skin makes its own cortisol and asks whether a cream could calm it. Which reading is right?
Explanation: Decide which direction the signal runs before you decide what to treat.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): Her skin's own cortisol explains the picture, so the answer is local.
Explanation: Local skin cortisol tunes immune activity where it is made. It does not explain new striae together with new hypertension.
Correct answer: The combination is a systemic pattern; the guide lists it as a reason for prompt endocrine referral before any skin treatment.
Explanation: Correct. Striae, bruising and new hypertension together point to possible systemic cortisol excess: a body-to-skin signal.

assertions.text: Locally produced skin cortisol regulates and tunes immune activity where it is synthesized.
assertions.quote: Independent work shows keratinocyte-derived, de novo glucocorticoids actively police local immune tone rather than merely echoing systemic cortisol.[5]
assertions.note: Supported by the pocket guide citing evidence on keratinocyte-derived glucocorticoids.

assertions.text: The combination of violaceous striae, skin thinning, and new hypertension points to systemic cortisol excess (suspected Cushing syndrome) and is listed as a reason for prompt endocrine referral.
assertions.quote: — Suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes).
assertions.note: Supported by the quick reference and referral criteria in the clinical pocket guide.

units.text:
Lesson 1.2 · Concept
A map of fourteen million cells.
The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers
Narration: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such …
units.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (published in Science in 2026) analyzed the RNA of 379 hormone and receptor genes across approximately 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, including skin.
assertions.quote: Drawing inspiration from the Human Cell Atlas, we analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in a transcriptomic dataset comprising 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms analyzing expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues.

assertions.text: The atlas mapped predicted capacity for cell types to produce or receive hormones based on RNA, rather than measuring active hormone secretion.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The portal and paper confirm these are transcriptomic predictions of putative hormone-producing and receiving cell types rather than functional hormone secretion measurements.

assertions.text: The study identified unexpected sites of hormone expression, including RNA for the gut hormone secretin in an immune cell type.
assertions.quote: We predicted nonclassical sites of hormone expression, including secretin in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, inferred convergent hormone action and endocrine feedback loops, and implicated cell populations in monogenic endocrine disorders.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly notes predicting nonclassical sites of hormone expression, including secretin in plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signaling networks due to containing every major cell lineage.
assertions.quote: Second, it follows that the skin — the body's largest organ, built from every major lineage (epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, adipocyte, immune, neural) in vast quantity — is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signaling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction rather than direct measurement of secretion.
assertions.note: Chapter 7 of the guide states this deduction directly.

units.text:
What the atlas is
Prediction, in the authors' own words.
The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
379
hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell
Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues
What it means: The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.
What it does not mean: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.
units.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran, Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk About/FAQ, read 24 Sep 2026 · Liu 2016

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal describes its scores and predictions as putative and hypothesis-generating.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal notes that predictions based on transcriptomic data should be considered putative and hypothesis-generating.

assertions.text: A few predictions were tested in vitro in the paper itself, while other predictions are left for users to validate.
assertions.quote: The user takes responsibility for validation using appropriate methods (e.g. in vitro, in vivo) and for describing appropriately their use of transcriptome-based scores and predictions.
assertions.note: The portal states that some predictions were investigated in vitro and users take responsibility for validating the rest.

assertions.text: Across biology, cellular RNA levels are frequently an insufficient guide to protein levels.
assertions.quote: We conclude that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios and to thus explain genotype-phenotype relationships and that high-quality data quantifying different levels of gene expression are indispensable for the complete understanding of biological processes.
assertions.note: The cited review concludes that transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios.

assertions.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes across roughly 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues.
assertions.quote: we analyzed the expression of 379 hormone and receptor genes in a transcriptomic dataset comprising 14 million single cells and nuclei across 47 human tissues.
assertions.note: The paper abstract confirms these exact dataset figures.

assertions.quote: Thus, even in the absence of endocrine, neural, or vascular systemic connections, normal human scalp hair follicles directly respond to CRH stimulation in a strikingly similar manner to what is seen in the classical HPA axis, including synthesis and secretion of cortisol and activation of prototypic neuroendocrine feedback loops.

assertions.note: Holick et al. describe the cutaneous synthesis of previtamin D3 upon solar exposure and the translocation of vitamin D3 into the circulation.

units.text:
What changes in practice
A map to confirm, then a trial.
Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.
A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D
Narration: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the d…
units.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

assertions.text: Topical and transdermal treatments act via the skin's native receptors, while local enzymes modify hormone potency such that the cutaneous response need not mirror the applied dose.
assertions.quote: Therapy: topical and transdermal routes exploit the skin's native receptors — retinoids (RAR), vitamin D analogs (VDR), estrogens (ER), glucocorticoids (GR) — but local steroid-metabolizing enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the systemic dose.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni notes that topical and transdermal routes use native skin receptors while local steroid-metabolizing enzymes alter potency.

assertions.text: Hannah-Shmouni's pocket guide states that serum 25-OH vitamin D falls with sunscreen use.
assertions.quote: Testing: serum 25-OH vitamin D partly reflects cutaneous synthesis, so it falls with low UVB exposure and sunscreen use regardless of oral intake.
assertions.note: Hannah-Shmouni's Chapter 7 testing pearl describes serum 25-OH vitamin D falling with sunscreen use.

assertions.text: Randomized controlled field trials found that daily sunscreen application did not lower circulating vitamin D levels.
assertions.quote: The randomized controlled field trials found no effect of daily sunscreen application, but the sunscreens used had moderate protection [sun protection factor SPF) ~16].
assertions.note: Neale et al. found that randomized controlled field trials showed no effect of daily sunscreen application on vitamin D levels.

assertions.text: The sunscreens tested in the field trials provided moderate protection, and high-SPF sunscreens have not been trialled.
assertions.quote: However, there have been no trials of the high-SPF sunscreens that are now widely recommended.
assertions.note: Neale et al. noted that the trials tested moderate protection (SPF ~16) and that high-SPF sunscreens have not been trialled.

units.text:
A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?
Explanation: A receptor on the map is where the question starts.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That the serum reaches those fibroblasts and improves the skin.
Explanation: That needs penetration data and a clinical trial; an RNA map provides neither.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That skin secretes the hormone and needs it replaced when levels fall.
Explanation: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.
Correct answer: That fibroblasts may respond to the hormone: a hypothesis to confirm at the protein, function and clinical level.
Explanation: Correct. The atlas's authors call such predictions putative and hypothesis-generating.

assertions.text: The authors of the single-cell hormone atlas characterize predictions based on transcriptomic data as putative and hypothesis-generating.
assertions.quote: Important: these predictions are based on transcriptomic data and should be considered as putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than as functional hormones and receptors.
assertions.note: The Hormone Cell Atlas portal explicitly notes that transcriptomic predictions should be considered putative and hypothesis-generating rather than functional.

units.text:
Lesson 1.3 · Concept
Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.
A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.
Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age
Narration: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as inte…
units.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

assertions.text: A senescent cell has permanently stopped dividing while remaining metabolically active and secreting cytokines, proteases/matrix-degrading enzymes, and growth factors (the SASP).
assertions.quote: Beyond remaining metabolically active, senescent cells develop a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) that can be rich in pro-inflammatory mediators, proteases, growth factors, extracellular components, aggregated or misfolded proteins (e.g., amyloid), bioactive molecules such as ROS, bradykines, or prostaglandins, and non-coding nucleotides, including micro-RNA’s and cell-free mitochondrial DNA.
assertions.note: Haykal et al. describe senescent cells as remaining metabolically active while releasing a secretome rich in pro-inflammatory mediators, proteases, and growth factors.

assertions.text: The senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) was characterized in human cell cultures following genotoxic stress and DNA damage.
assertions.quote: We show that human cells induced to senesce by genotoxic stress secrete myriad factors associated with inflammation and malignancy. This senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) developed slowly over several days and only after DNA damage of sufficient magnitude to induce senescence.
assertions.note: Coppé et al. characterized the SASP using cultured human cells induced to senesce following genotoxic stress and DNA damage.

assertions.text: In human skin, cells expressing the senescence biomarker p16INK4a increase with age across both the epidermis and dermis.
assertions.quote: The number of p16INK4A positive cells was found to be increased in both epidermis and dermis, compartments with strictly different proliferative activities.
assertions.note: Ressler et al. observed significant increases in p16-positive cells with age across both dermal and epidermal compartments.

assertions.text: Senescence functions initially as a protective mechanism guarding against cancer and assisting in wound repair.
assertions.quote: Initially evolved as a protective mechanism to prevent malignant transformation and facilitate wound repair, senescence becomes maladaptive when senescent cells persist.
assertions.note: Haykal et al. note that cellular senescence evolved as a protective response against malignant transformation and to aid wound healing.

assertions.text: Fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and melanocytes can all undergo cellular senescence in skin.
assertions.quote: Senescent keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and melanocytes can secrete pro-inflammatory mediators and other factors, collectively termed the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which may degrade extracellular matrix components, disrupt pigmentary balance, and impair barrier function.
assertions.note: Haykal et al. describe senescent keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and melanocytes developing a SASP in skin.

assertions.text: No single biomarker identifies a senescent cell with unequivocal certainty.
assertions.quote: The identification of unique markers that unequivocally detect and quantify senescent cells, particularly in vivo , remains challenging ( Sharpless and Sherr, 2015 ).
assertions.note: Wang & Dreesen note that identifying a universal marker to unequivocally detect senescent cells in vivo remains challenging.

units.text:
Human evidence
Three years of perceived age.
In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
3 years
younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age
Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies
What it means: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.
What it does not mean: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.
units.sourceNote: Waaijer 2016 (Leiden Longevity Study) · Ressler 2006

assertions.text: In a study of 178 adults aged 45–81 in the Leiden Longevity Study, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles, and looked older, after adjusting for chronological age.
assertions.quote: The numbers of epidermal and dermal p16INK4a positive cells were significantly associated with age-associated elastic fiber morphologic characteristics, such as longer and a greater number of elastic fibers. The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm biopsies from 178 participants were significantly associated with age-related elastic fiber morphology, facial wrinkles, and higher perceived age after adjusting for chronological age.

assertions.text: The epidermal p16-positive cells were primarily melanocytes.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: The abstract explicitly states that p16-positive epidermal cells were identified primarily as melanocytes.

assertions.text: Participants in the lowest tertile of p16-positive epidermal cells looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile, at the same chronological age.
assertions.quote: Participants in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16INK4a counts looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile, independently of chronological age and elastic fiber morphology.
assertions.note: The abstract confirms that participants in the lowest tertile looked 3 years younger than those in the highest tertile independently of chronological age.

assertions.text: The study was publicly funded and one co-author worked for Unilever.
assertions.note: Funding and author affiliation details are not present in the provided abstract.

units.text:
Four registers
Human, mouse or dish?
Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
Mechanism
A collagen-fragmentation loop
Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
Human evidence
Association
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Animal evidence
Causation, in mice
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.
Open question
Do senotherapies change human skin?
Small pilots measuring tissue markers. One exp…
units.sourceNote: Shuster 1975 · Varani 2006 · Fisher 2009 · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Xu 2018 · Hickson 2019 · Chung 2019

assertions.text: Skin collagen falls with age.
assertions.quote: Skin collagen decreased with age and was less in the females at all ages.
assertions.note: Skin collagen decreases with age.

assertions.text: Aged human dermis shows increased MMP-1 and collagen fragmentation, and cultured fibroblasts in fragmented collagen upregulate MMP-1 further.
assertions.quote: Furthermore, fibroblasts cultured in fragmented collagen lattices express elevated levels of MMP-1, AP-1, and alpha2beta1 integrin.
assertions.note: Fibroblasts in aged skin in vivo and those cultured in fragmented collagen express elevated MMP-1.

assertions.text: p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age.
assertions.quote: The p16INK4a positive epidermal cells (identified as primarily melanocytes) were also significantly associated with more facial wrinkles and a higher perceived age.
assertions.note: Epidermal p16-positive cells correlate with facial wrinkling and higher perceived age.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells or administering senolytics extends healthy lifespan in mice.
assertions.quote: Thus, p16 Ink4a -positive cells that accumulate during adulthood negatively influence lifespan and promote age-dependent changes in multiple organs, and their therapeutic removal may be an attractive approach to extend healthy lifespan.
assertions.note: Targeted removal of p16-positive cells in mice extends healthy lifespan.

assertions.text: Clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure in mice.
assertions.quote: When AP was administered during wound closure, healing was delayed with similar kinetics as 4- or 18-month-old ATTAC mice without prior AP treatment, indicating that acute senescence mechanisms are preserved with aging and not influenced by constitutive clearance of senescent cells 3 .
assertions.note: Administration of the clearance dimerizer during wound repair delayed wound closure.

assertions.text: In an exploratory trial of topical rapamycin, 36 participants were enrolled and 19 dropped out, with treatment lowering skin p16.
assertions.quote: Thirty-six participants were enrolled, and nineteen discontinued or were lost to follow-up. A significant ( P = 0.008) reduction in p16 INK4A protein levels and an increase in collagen VII protein levels ( P = 0.0077) were observed among participants at the end of the study.
assertions.note: Thirty-six participants enrolled, 19 discontinued/were lost to follow-up, and p16 expression was reduced.

units.text:
Where the evidence is strongest
The levers with trials behind them.
Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.
Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet
Narration: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded …
units.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

assertions.text: In a randomized community trial of 903 adults over 4.5 years, daily sunscreen slowed skin aging by approximately 24% compared with discretionary use.
assertions.quote: Skin aging from baseline to the end of the trial was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group than in the discretionary sunscreen group (relative odds, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.59 to 0.98]).
assertions.note: The Nambour community trial in 903 adults found skin aging was 24% less in the daily sunscreen group compared to discretionary use over 4.5 years.

assertions.text: Topical tretinoin consistently improves clinical signs of photoaging across randomized controlled trials.
assertions.quote: With regard to efficacy, all studies consistently reported that topical tretinoin was efficacious in improving clinical appearance of photoaging in terms of wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, sallowness, and lentigines as early as 1 month and lasted after 24 months.
assertions.note: A systematic review of randomized trials showed consistent efficacy of topical tretinoin for photoaging.

assertions.text: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line with GRADE A evidence for reversing photoaging.
assertions.quote: Among topical agents, retinoids have the strongest dermatologic evidence for reversing measurable signs of photoaging and remain first-line GRADE A.
assertions.note: The guide designates retinoids as first-line with GRADE A evidence.

assertions.text: Topical retinol improved fine wrinkling and increased procollagen I in a randomized trial of elderly individuals with a mean age of 87 years.
assertions.quote: After 24 weeks, an intent-to-treat analysis using the last-observation-carried-forward method revealed that there were significant differences between retinol-treated and vehicle-treated skin for changes in fine wrinkling scores (-1.64 [95% CI, -2.06 to -1.22] vs -0.08 [95% CI, -0.17 to 0.01]; P<.001).
assertions.note: A randomized trial in 36 elderly subjects (mean age 87) showed significant improvement in fine wrinkling and increased procollagen I immunostaining.

assertions.text: Topical retinol application for 7 days increased collagen synthesis and reduced matrix metalloproteinases in biopsies of aged human skin.
assertions.quote: In a separate group of 53 individuals (80+ y of age), topical application of 1% vitamin A for 7 d increased fibroblast growth and collagen synthesis, and concomitantly reduced the levels of matrix-degrading matrix metalloproteinases.
assertions.note: Biopsies from subjects aged 80+ treated with topical vitamin A for 7 days showed increased collagen synthesis and reduced matrix metalloproteinases.

assertions.text: There are no clinical outcome trials yet for senolytics targeting skin aging.
assertions.quote: Senolytics belong in trials. The preclinical story is compelling; human outcome evidence is not yet there.
assertions.note: The pocket guide notes that senolytic strategies have compelling preclinical data but skin-specific human outcome evidence is not yet established.

'Can a senolytic fix my skin?'
A 58-year-old patient has read that senolytic supplements 'clear zombie cells' and reverse skin ageing, and asks whether to start one she found online. She does not use sunscreen daily. The case is fictional and built from the lesson's evidence; decide your first move.
Senescent cells in human skin: real, and linked with visible ageing
Clearing them: mouse evidence and small human biomarker pilots
Sunscreen and retinoids: randomized human trials
