units.text: Signs of growth-hormone excess include puffy, thickened skin of the face, hands and feet, oily skin, more sweating, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, tight rings or shoes, night-time tingling and carpal tunnel symptoms. On GH-axis drugs, fluid retention with swelling and joint pain is common and usually settles when treatment stops. The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 testing when typical acral and facial features are present, so route these patients to a prescriber or to endocrinology. On cancer, keep four answers apart: the IGF-1 receptor drives cell growth (mechanism); higher natural IGF-1 goes with modestly higher risk of some cancers (observation); GH replacement in true deficiency has not shown a clear risk in large cohorts; and for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for skin, long-term cancer data do not exist (open question).

assertions.text: Signs of growth hormone excess include puffy skin of the face, hands, and feet, oily skin, increased sweating, skin tags, and acanthosis nigricans.
assertions.quote: Skin puffiness due to dermal glycosaminoglycan accumulation and edema are most prominent in the face, hands and feet. Oily skin with large pores, hypertrichosis, and excessive sweating are common features. Pigmented skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, and psoriasis are also encountered.
assertions.note: The abstract details skin puffiness of the face, hands, and feet, oily skin, excessive sweating, skin tags, and acanthosis nigricans in acromegaly.

assertions.text: On GH-axis drugs, fluid retention manifesting with swelling and joint pain occurs and usually settles when treatment stops.
assertions.quote: Fluid retention may occur during EGRIFTA WR therapy and is thought to be related to the induction of GH secretion. This manifests as increased tissue turgor and musculoskeletal discomfort resulting in adverse reactions (e.g. edema, arthralgia, and carpal tunnel syndrome) which are either transient or resolve with discontinuation of treatment.
assertions.note: The prescribing label confirms fluid retention adverse reactions such as edema and arthralgia are transient or resolve with discontinuation.

assertions.text: The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 testing when typical acral and facial features are present.
assertions.note: The provided abstract mentions addressing biochemical assessment generally, but does not state this specific recommendation.

recheck.note: The provided abstract for the Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline does not contain the specific recommendation details regarding IGF-1 testing for typical acral and facial features.

assertions.text: Higher circulating IGF-1 concentrations are associated with a modestly increased risk of certain cancers.
assertions.quote: Circulating concentrations of IGF-I and IGFBP-3 are associated with an increased risk of common cancers, but associations are modest and vary between sites.
assertions.note: The meta-analysis abstract notes modest associations between circulating IGF-1 concentrations and increased risk of common cancers.

assertions.text: GH replacement in patients with growth failure/deficiency has not demonstrated a clear overall cancer risk in large cohorts.
assertions.quote: There was no clear raised risk in patients with growth failure without other major disease.
assertions.note: The SAGhE European cohort study found no clear raised cancer risk in patients treated for growth failure without other major disease.

units.text: GRADE rates certainty for a specific outcome across a body of evidence: high, moderate, low or very low (the Hormonaly guides print A to D). Randomized trials start high; certainty drops for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias. Industry-sponsored studies more often report favourable results (Cochrane, 2017), so ask who ran and paid for the trials. A grade is separate from legal status: check both, and never let a mechanism raise a grade. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice.

assertions.text: GRADE rates certainty across a body of evidence into four categories: high, moderate, low, or very low (represented as A to D in the Hormonaly guides).
assertions.quote: GRADE specifies four categories-high, moderate, low, and very low-that are applied to a body of evidence, not to individual studies.
assertions.note: GRADE categorizes evidence quality/certainty across a body of evidence into high, moderate, low, and very low.

assertions.text: In GRADE, randomized trials start at high certainty, but certainty can decrease due to risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias.
assertions.quote: Randomized trials begin as high-quality evidence, observational studies as low quality. "Quality" as used in GRADE means more than risk of bias and so may also be compromised by imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness of study results, and publication bias.
assertions.note: Randomized trials start high and can be downgraded for imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, publication bias, or risk of bias.

assertions.text: Industry-sponsored research more frequently yields favorable results compared with non-industry-sponsored research.
assertions.quote: Sponsorship of drug and device studies by the manufacturing company leads to more favorable efficacy results and conclusions than sponsorship by other sources.
assertions.note: The Cochrane review found that industry sponsorship leads to more favorable efficacy results and conclusions.

assertions.text: Evidentiary GRADE ratings are separate from regulatory status, and mechanistic appeal alone does not raise an evidence grade.
assertions.quote: An FDA-approved drug may carry a lower grade for a particular off-label use than an investigational compound supported by stronger human evidence; regulatory status and evidentiary certainty are separate axes. Mechanistic appeal alone never raises a grade.
assertions.note: Regulatory status and evidentiary certainty are distinct axes, and mechanism alone never raises a grade.

units.text: In the US, a 503A pharmacy may compound only from a substance that meets a USP or NF monograph, or else is a component of an approved drug, or else is on the 503A bulks list (six substances, none a peptide, as of September 2026), and it needs a valid certificate of analysis. A certificate is the supplier's report on one lot: mass spectrometry for identity, HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin and microbial results. It cannot prove your vial is that lot, how it was stored, or that it is sterile or lawful. 'Research use only' products are labelled not for use in humans, and 'off-label' applies only to approved drugs. assertions.text: In the US, a 503A pharmacy may compound only from bulk drug substances meeting a USP or NF monograph, components of an approved drug, or substances on the 503A bulks list, accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis.
assertions.quote: comply with the standards of an applicable United States Pharmacopoeia or National Formulary monograph, if a monograph exists, and the United States Pharmacopoeia chapter on pharmacy compounding ; (II) if such a monograph does not exist, are drug substances that are components of drugs approved by the Secretary ; or (III) if such a monograph does not exist and the drug substance is not a component
assertions.note: 21 U.S.C. § 353a requires bulk drug substances to meet a USP/NF monograph, be components of approved drugs, or appear on the 503A bulks list, and be accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis.

assertions.text: The 503A bulks list contains six substances, none of which is a peptide (as of 2026).
assertions.quote: The 503A bulks list is codified at 21 C.F.R. 216.23 and holds six substances — Brilliant Blue G, cantharidin, diphenylcyclopropenone, N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, squaric acid dibutyl ester, thymol iodide — four topical-only. No peptide is on it.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 216.23 lists exactly six bulk substances, none of which is a peptide.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis is the supplier's report on one lot, providing mass spectrometry for identity, HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin and microbial results.
assertions.quote: A serious COA tells you what the supplier found on a named lot: whether the mass matches the expected molecule, how pure the material was by HPLC, what counter-ion it carries, and what the endotoxin and microbial results were.
assertions.note: The Peptide Pocket Guide describes a certificate of analysis as covering lot-specific mass spectrometry, HPLC purity, and microbial/endotoxin results.

assertions.text: A certificate of analysis cannot prove that a vial is from that lot, how it was stored, or that it is sterile or lawful.
assertions.quote: What it cannot establish on its own is that a product is safe to inject — that turns on sterility, the dose and route, the conditions the material was held in since testing, and whether the lot tested is the lot in hand.
assertions.note: The source notes that a COA alone cannot verify post-testing conditions, sterility to inject, or lot matching.

assertions.text: 'Research use only' products are labelled not for use in humans.
assertions.quote: CAUTION: Contains a new drug for investigational use only in laboratory research animals, or for tests in vitro. Not for use in humans.
assertions.note: 21 CFR 312.160 requires research/in vitro products to be labeled 'Not for use in humans.'

assertions.text: 'Off-label' use applies only to unapproved uses of approved drugs.
assertions.quote: Unapproved use of an approved drug is often called “off-label” use.
assertions.note: FDA guidance defines off-label use specifically as an unapproved use of an approved drug.

assertions.text: In the UK, an unlicensed medicine reaches a patient as a 'special' made to a prescriber's order for an individual patient's special clinical need, or prepared by a pharmacist against a prescription.
assertions.quote: This Guidance Note provides advice on the manufacture, importation, distribution and supply of unlicensed medicinal products for human use (commonly described as “specials”) which have been specially manufactured or imported to the order of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber for the treatment of individual patients.
assertions.note: MHRA Guidance Note 14 and Section 10 of the Medicines Act 1968 outline specials manufacturing and pharmacy preparation routes.

assertions.text: MHRA guidance ranks a UK-licensed medicine, even when used off-label, ahead of an unlicensed medicine.
assertions.quote: Although MHRA does not recommend “off-label” (outside the licensed indications) use of products, if a UK licensed product can meet the clinical need, even off-label, it should be used instead of an unlicensed product (see Appendix 2).
assertions.note: MHRA guidance explicitly states that an off-label UK-licensed medicine should be preferred over an unlicensed product.

assertions.text: Specials may not be advertised in the UK.
assertions.quote: (3) Condition B is that no advertisement relating to the medicinal product is published by any person.
assertions.note: Under UK Human Medicines Regulations 2012 reg 167(3), no advertisement relating to a special may be published.
